Bill (No. 6) to amend the Railway Act.- Mr. Lancaster.

Mr. JOHN BARR (Dufferin) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 32) to amend the Railway Act. He said:	Mr. Speaker,
in moving the second reading of this Bill I would like to remind the House that last year I explained the object of the measure and, although there are many new members who were not in the House then, I do not intend to trespass at any great length upon the time of the House on the present occasion. The object of this Bill is to facilitate the crossing of railways by lines or wires

for telegraphs or telephones, or for conveyance of light, heat, power, or electricity, and by water mains, conduits, and sewers. As the law stands at the present time, in order to extend any of these public utilities across a railway, it is necessary for an individual or company to make application to the railway authorities. In many cases great delay is caused. I do not believe it is necessary that such should be the case, but those who are interested in these crossings often experience delavs in receiving an answer from the railway companies of from one to four weeks. When the answer comes back it usually is that permission will be given to cross on payment of $5. I think this is all wrong. I have on every occasion objected to the suggestion that the people should be compelled to pay anything for a crossing which they have a right to. Hon. gentlemen are aware that in 99 cases out of 100 these crossings are on the public highway in towns and villages, or on side roads and concessions in the rural districts. The railways do not own these highways. They belonged to the municipalities long before the railways were built, and it seems to me to be an outrage that the people should be asked to pay $5 for what belongs to them. The railways have no power over these highways. All they possess is the right, obtained from the charter granted by this House, to cross these highways under certain restrictions. The provisions of this Bill are that an individual or company asking to be allowed to cross a highway shall give notice to the railway authorities, to the station master, or if there is no station master in the municipality, to the official most convenient. If the company do not take action within fifteen days the individual or company making application may cross the railway according to regulations laid down by the Board of Railway Commissioners.
In this there could be no hardship so far as the railroads are concerned. The instructions from the Railroad Board protect the railroads by requiring that a certain kind of wire shall be strung and that the arms and poles must be in acordance with the rules and regulations. Thus there could be no reason for not granting this Bill.
As to sewers, viaducts, conduits and water pipes which pass under the railroads, I have provided in this Bill, in accordance with the direction of the Railway Board in a number of cases, that in the event of municipalities or individuals crossing a railroad by water pipes or sewers, &c., the engineer of the railway company must approve of the method of crossing and must be paid by the party making the crossing, the charge not to exceed $5. This is the amount awarded in several cases in which I was interested, and as the engineer's time would not generally be occupied for more than an hour, it seems to be a fair charge.
This Bill has been demanded by the people in every part of Canada. When I introduced it last year it was printed in the Municipal Journal and I had many letters from every province, a few of which I read to the House, approving of the Bill. Since this Bill was printed I have received a number of letters which I shall not trouble the House by reading. Hon. gentlemen are aware that in cases of crossing railroads with water pipes, &c., the railways demand not only the $5 but also a lease of $1 a year for all time to come from the municipality or individual, which appears to me to be ridiculous. We have had demands of that kind in the village of Shelburne; we refused to accede to them and application was made to the Railway Commission; but the commissioners were busy at the time and we were delayed for some six or seven months.
The telephone is a utility whose use is increasing very rapidly. In the four years during which the Railway Commission has existed the number of applications for crossings by telephone lines was 2,411 and the number granted 2,328. None were refused, showing that the railroads should have granted those crossings without putting the applicants to the trouble and expense of an application to the Board. During last year there were 1,025 applications of this character to the Railway Commission and I submit that if this Bill goes through it will take a great deal of work off the Railway Commission, which we have heard is overworked. At the time when farmers are building their telephone lines, the Railway Commissioners are usually on their holidays and by the time they return to their offices a large amount of work has accumulated so that there is unnecessary delay to the farmers in securing permission to cross the railroads. Then an application to the Railway Commission entails great expense, particularly upon the small companies which are threading their telephone throughout the country. The telephone has done a great deal for this country. It has united the cities, towns and villages with the country and has made country life much more easy, much more fascinating to the young and rising generation and has had the effect of keeping many young men on the farms who would otherwise not remain there. Under these circumstances I think we should facilitate as far as possible the building of those telephone lines. I had hoped that the time would not be far distant when the telephone lines would be taken over by the provincial or Dominion government. The province of Manitoba has taken over the Bell telephone lines there and I was glad to see the announcement of the Prime Minister of Manitoba that during the past year their telephones have been a paying asset to the province and that they are determined to push the work as rapidly as

possible and build telephones throughout that province. If Manitoba can make the telephone a paying speculation, there is no reason why other provinces should not do so and why it should not be a still greater success if the Dominion parliament should take hold of it and operate it. Some years ago, after weeks of personal investigation before a committee, Sir William Mulock stated that it was the intention of the gov-enment to bring in a Bill the following year to take over the telephones and run them in connection with the post office. If we had a telephone in every post office and in every farm house where they desired to pay a reasonable price, it would be a great boon to the rural population of Canada. That project did not materialize but whilst we have not these advantages, whilst we are not advancing as rapidly as the province of Manitoba in this respect, I hope that the good example of Manitoba will be followed by other provinces.
While that is the case I submit that it is our duty to facilitate the building of these telephone lines as quickly as possible. In connection with these 1.025 crossings during the last year, if the railway companies had been able to carry out their designs, they would have pocketed over $5,000 of the people's money. I think that should be prevented, and I have a clause in the Bill prohibiting the railway companies from demanding any money from the people on this account. There is no reason why they should. In every case of such a crossing the people are put to considerable expense. They have first to make their application to the Commission, then they have to send a duplicate of the plans and specifications, and in some cases they have to employ a lawyer or some other person to take the necessary proceedings. All this should be avoided. There is no reason why they should be put either to delay or to expense. Under these circumstances I would ask the government to allow this Bill to have a second reading and then to go to a committee, as was agreed to last year-either the Railway Committee or some other committee; and any improvements that can be made to the Bill I can assure you I shall be glad to give careful consideration to, so that it may be made as perfect as possible. I think I have stated the case fairly enough to show beyond a doubt that there is a grievance and that there should be a remedy, which can easily be worked out, and I think this Bill fairly meets the requirements of the case.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this Bill, as my hon. friend has remarked, is not a new one; it has been in the House before, but as this is a new parliament and there are a large number of representatives who have not been here before, perhaps the House will bear with me while I say a

few words upon it. My hon. friend has discussed the question of the provinces or the Dominion taking over the telephone lines. That is a large subject, and I have no objection at all to my hon. friend impressing it upon his friends in the provincial legislatures or upon my friends where they have the supremacy in the provinces. The policy adopted by the Parliament of Canada has been government control through the Board of Railway Commission- . ers over telephones, telegraphs, express companies and railway companies; and this year that power is to be extended along another line. A year ago I had the honour to introduce an amendment to the Railway Act, which brought telephone companies under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and that part of the Act was brought into force by order in council. It was not brought into force at once owing to some representations having been made to me which appeared to satisfy the House on that point. That order in council was passed some little time ago, and to-day telephone companies are under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The gist of my hon. friend's Bill is that any company, either a telephone company, a telegraph company or a municipality, can, without any reference to the Board of Railway Commissioners or to the company concerned, string their wires across a railway or run their pipes under the track. Now, I submit to the House that that is a very serious proposition. At the present moment the question of the safety of the people travelling on our highways is engaging the attention of this House and of the country, and we must be very careful to do nothing to increase the danger to the travelling public either on the highways or on the railways.
I have discussed this matter very thoroughly with some men who ought to know, and they tell me that it would be a very great source of danger if every person who thought he knew how to string a wire were allowed to string wires across a railway track near the wires of the railway company, without the supervision of some competent person to see that it was done properly. A great many accidents from fire are said to be caused by the improper wiring of houses, and a great deal of danger might be caused by the improper placing of a wire by inexperienced people across a railway track, where it might come in contact with the wires already there, or, if loosely strung, with the trains.
Cannot any farmer measure six feet?

We might ask the same question about the insulation of wires; but there is a proper way and an improper way, a proper place and an improper place for stringing wires. This matter has been

placed in the hands of the Railway Commissioners, who are the servants of the public, and there it ought to be left. My hon. friend will not say that during the past year he had to wait six months for any reply to his communication. My hon. friend said that it occurred a year ago, so that it must have been the same case that he referred to before; it could not have occurred within the past year. I think all such matters have been dealt with promptly within the last few months, and they will be in the future. With regard to pipes under the railway tracks, I am not an advocate of the railway companies at all, but on behalf of the public I think this is a case in which the greatest care ought to be exercised. The railway companies ought certainly to be notified in every case, and if they have something to say as to whether an application should be granted or not, they should have an opportunity to show where and how the pipes should go. Several cases of this kind have been brought to my knowledge. In some cases it is sought to put pipes under railway tracks where the ground is springy, and consequently where the roadbed might be seriously affected and an accident caused to the travelling public. These are reasons for leaving the matter under the control of the Railway Commissioners, in whom we have confidence. I have no objecion to the Bill going to the committee, but nothing has been said to change my mind or I believe the mind of this House as to the importance of exercising the utmost care in allowing wires to be strung across railway tracks or allowing pipes to be put under them, and this care can best be exercised by the men we have appointed for the purpose, that is, the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph lines.

They will be a very lengthy printed document. The only part which would be of much benefit to the House would be the report of the commissioners themselves. What means has this government of producing the report of the government of the province of New Brunswick?
It is on the table.
Why then move for a return? I thought the intention was to move that it be printed.
I made the motion in order to put it in order for printing. While the papers are already on the table, they are not regularly so with the view of having it printed.

Before the motion carries, I would like to ask the Minister of Railways if he is prepared to tell me now

whether that reference alluded to by the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) in 1902, when he said there would be a reference to the courts to ascertain the actual cost of the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, has ever been acted on?

Will the hon. gentleman bring down the order in council itself which was made in 1902 and which corresponds with the order in council increasing the capital stock?
Yes.
