' Pension to Mrs. Elizabeth Wilmot, $51.75.
['If my hon. friend desires I will bring them all down.']

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is a new item and the pension was granted under these circumstances. Constable George Ernest Wilmot, Royal Northwest Mounted Police was murdered while on duty at Frank, Alberta, on the morning of the 12th of April, 1908, by some person or persons unknown. Up to the present time no clue to the murder has been obtained. During the first days of April, 1908, a number of burglaries took place in Frank and Sergeant Haslett arranged with constable Wilmot to patrol the town at night to try to capture the criminals. On Saturday night April, the 11th, Sergeant Haslett came off duty at 12.30 being relieved by constable Wilmot and about 7 a.m. the following morning constable Wilmot's body was found lying in an alley-way behind the hotel at Frank. There were gaping wounds on the neck and chest caused by gun shot. Mrs. Elizabeth Wilmot, mother of the deceased, is a widow residing in England and she applied for compensation for the loss of her son on whom Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
she was entirely dependent for support. There is evidence that the deceased was in the habit of sending her money from his police pay. She has two sons living, one of whom is married and has a home of his own and the other is an inmate of an epileptic home. These facts were sworn to before a Justice of the Peace. Following the usual practice in existence since 1885, and, it being a most deserving case, we granted to the mother a pension of one-half constable Wilmot's pay.
Surely Constable Wilmot was paid more than $108 a year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is based on 365 days' pay at 30 cents a day.
Is no cognizance taken of the value of his rations and uniform ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I followed the rule that has been in existence since 1885.
And that is all the pension the poor woman gets ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is all.

The rule followed by private corporations which grant pensions is to take into consideration the value of house rent and fuel where such allowances are made and to add their value to the salary. These things are always taken into consideration in granting a pension to the family of a deceased officer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not dispute that nor do I say it is not a sound rule, but I found this rule in the department and I adhered to it.
Penitentiaries, $507,350.
Is this intended to cover all the expenditure on penitentiaries for the year 1909-10 ?
It is supposed to cover all the expenditure for the year.
There is quite a large increase in the expenditure for Dorchester penitentiary.
That increase was caused by the installation of an electric light plant in the penitentiary.
Will this be a permanent increase ?
Yes.
Was this plant installed by the government itself; is this amount simply for the cost of wiring ?
This is the difference in price between lighting by coal oil as formerly and lighting by electric light. It costs us $1,000 more to light by electricity than by coal oil.
What arrangement was made between the government and the electric light company as to installation and electric wiring and so on.

The wiring and installation was done by the convicts and there was no charge for outside labour. We pay 8 cents per kilowatt for the light. There is $1,000 for increase of salaries and the other $1,000 increase is for electricity.
I w.ould like to find out, if I can, what was the entire cost of the installation of the electric lighting.
We purchased the material and the labour was done by the convicts.
Perhaps the solicitor general would bring the information down at a later date ?

The Auditor General's Report will show what supplies were purchased and I will have to get information as to the number of hours the convicts worked on the job and the estimated value of their labour.
May I ask what the arrangement is for the electric light the company has to supply ?
8 cents per kilowatt.
Can you make it as little as you choose, or as much as you choose, cr does the contract call for the acceptance of any quantity they may choose to give you?
We take it by meter.
You can stop the service any time you choose?
There is a contract for five years, but there is no minimum or maximum amount we are bound to take. We take only what we consume.
Then you are not bound to take any.
Except what we consume.
Can you cut off the service any time you choose?
No, we have a five years contract.
Are you bound to take a certain quantity of electricity from the company in any event?
I told my hon. friend that there was no minimum amount that we were bound to take, and no maximum amount either. We take what we require, and pay for what we take.
What is the estimated cost of lighting the penitentiary per year?
What was the previous annual amount for light before you installed electricity?
$700, and we add $1,000 more for electricity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the committee please confine their attention to the first item,'$3,000 for the general vote?
Will the Solicitor General explain the decrease of $9,000 in that general vote?

There are two inspectors, a parole officer and one architect, that are mentioned in the estimates. Last year their salaries totalled $8,400. These are transferred from penitentiaries to civil government.
How do you propose to expend the other $3,000?

The expense of the parole officer is $1,700, assistance to paroled and discharged convicts, $300, for office contingencies, $1,000.
Kingston penitentiary, $151,200.

I ask the minister to look at the items mentioned in the Auditor General's Report L-17:
Frontenac Lumber & Coal Co., Kingston: cement, 152 barrels at $2; cartage on same, $12.90; hemlock lumber, 10,005 ft. at $22.50; cedar posts, 100 at 20c.; cordwood, 21 cords at $4.50; oak, 10 ft., 80c.; total, $657.32.
Were all these goods purchased by tender?

They were not purchased by tender. Quotations were asked from various dealers, ani these were the lowest figures that were offered. We have no patronage list in the Department of Justice, and never had.

Then I want the Solicitor General to draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the fact that here at Ottawa where cement is made, he got 86 barrels for his work on the astronomical building and paid $2.50 for it; and the Minister of Railways purchased his at Montreal at $1.65
The Minister of Railways bought by the carload, and got it cheaper

That shows how political friends have a pull. At Kingston they only get $2 a barrel; here at Ottawa they get $2.50. I do not see why the government should not make a rule, and pay the same price all round. Then turn to page L-18, and the minister will find a purchase from Alphonse Racine & Co., Montreal, amounting to $2,436, principally for dry goods. Were these purchased by tender?
Yes, those were purchased by tender. Public tenders are asked for through the press.
At Kingston the minister paid $22.50 per thousand for hemlock lumber. Is he not aware that hemlock lumber is not worth more than $13?
I suppose it all depends on the lumber.
It all depends upon whom you buy it from.
This was dimension lumber that was required for the repair of a wharf, and that is the reason that we paid a little higher price for it.
For dimension lumber it_ ought to be a great deal less. For repairing a wharf you simply need square pieces. I have had a good deal to do with wharf building.
In these eases prices were invited, and that is the best price we could get. The prices were invited from the local dealers, friend and foe.
If there were no advertisements in the paper, only the friends could know.
We send them a notice asking for prices.
Does the Solicitor General say that notices were sent to all the local dealers inviting them to tender.
I am informed there are only three or four dealers in Kingston, and (he notice was sent to each of them. Anyway, we gave instructions to ask the dealers for prices.
I find that our friends the McAvitys of St. John are down for quite a large order for supplies for the penitentiaries. Were tenders invited from them?
Quotations were asked from the hardware merchants, Robertsons of Montreal, who have a house in St. John, and the McAvitys. The McAvitys prices were the lower, I am informed by the inspector.
What other firms were invited to tender in St. John outside of the McAvity firm.
Jas. Robertson & Co. and McAvity were the only two from whom prices were asked.

All the other hardware dealers in St. John and New Brunswick were not asked?
Mr. BUREAU I am informed not.
And yet the Solicitor General says the Justice Department has no patronage list.
There is none.
I notice you are dealing with the same bunch as the other departments.
These are two of the largest houses in the Dominion, and the prices quoted by smaller houses could not be any better.

I think this is an opportune moment for finding out, if we possibly can, what the government means and whether it is playing to the gallery and concealing what it is actually doing. In the last two or three weeks an impression has gone broadcast, through the publication of Mr Justice Cassels' report, that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had done away with the patronage system. I am not sure that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries anywhere said that he did away with the patronage system. The communication, as I find it, is that he had instructed that the present patronage lists be done away with. That has gone broadcast through the country and the press supporting the hon. gentleman opposite are heralding it as a great and important reform, that now the government, seeing the error of its ways, has determined to do the square thing and have no more of this system of patronage. I looked at the communication which was sent by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to Judge Cassels, through Mr. Watson, and it was accorded a very prominent place in the report, for what reason I do not know, and the essence of it, boiled down, is simply that the minister had instructed that the present patronage lists should be dispensed with. Now, we ought to have the same method of dealing by the government through all its departments. I think my right hon. friend the Prime Minister will bear me out in that statement. On the question of public policy what one department does the other department ought to do. If the patronage system is wrong and something else should be substituted _ in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the same method of dealing should hold in the other departments. I do not think the right hon. gentleman will controvert that statement. The Solicitor General has, by a concrete instance, shown that the patronage list is not abolished in reference to his department. He has not even gone as far as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
That was a year ago.
This is one of the items that we are discussing now, and in this particular case only two firms have been asked for tenders in the city of St. John.
That was a year ago.

One in St. John and one in Montreal.
Mr. BUREAU Robertson is in St. John also.
Then, there were two in St. John.
That was last year.

That was last year? That is the patronage list. The Solicitor General says there never was a patronage list in the Justice Department. There seems to be a patronage list. I know, of my own personal knowledge of St. John, a number of excellent firms that are engaged in dealing in hardware. I think we ought to have now a declaration of the policy of the government and I think I can bring it out by two questions Will the Prime Minister tell us that, by the abolition of the present patronage lists in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, that department has abolished the patronage system? That is one question. The other question is:	Are the reasons which led
the Department of Marine and Fisheries to abolish the patronage system if he has done so good enough to base the action of other departments of the government upon? Is the whole government, in the purchase of these supplies, going to abolish the patronage lists and the patronage system, one or the other, or both? The Solicitor General's reply is that in so far as the work is concerned which he is explaining, they have not abolished the patronage list or the patronage system.

The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster; takes advantage of this item to say that we have been exercising very little discretion in our purchases, but, looking over these items, purchased from McAvity & Sons, I find that they are all for very small amounts, that they were purchased at various times, and that the total is $1,109 for the year. I see that there were 150 feet of asbestos pipe covering at 15% cents per foot purchased from that firm. Does my hon. friend mean to say that we should ask tenders through the press, or from every dealer, whenever there is a small repair to be made or a small quantity of anything required? I am informed by the inspector that these houses of Robertson and McAvity are two of the strongest houses in Canada and that getting prices from them would be a fair indication of the lowest prices that could be got from any one. These small purchases were made from time to time as occasion required. Prices were asked from Robertson and McAvity, and McAvity's prices being the lower, the purchases were made from them.

The Solicitor General has taken care not to answer at all the question that I asked. I am not going to lay up against him as a crime the bad practice of the past, but will he tell me if, for the future, the department whose estimates he is explaining now will do away with the patronage list and the patronage system as it has been carried on in the past?

I would like to ask my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) what system he would suggest adopting in the case of small purchases. In the case of the Department of Marine agency at Halifax some few weeks ago a list of the supplies wanted during the current year was made up. The public were asked to tender in some cases for one fog horn or one paint brush. There were numerous instances where but one article of a particular class was required How would the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) deal with purchases of this kind unless he leaves the matter to the judgment of some officer or agency of the department? Surely he would not insist on public advertisements for such supplies. I think the department has adopted a very good and businesslike method, where the quantity is so small, in asking two reputable business houses to furnish prices, and where the quantity is large in asking the public for tenders.

I shall answer my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean), who seems to occupy the place of the devil's advocate in this, after the answers have been given by the minister who is explaining the estimates. I never knew a system or principle of any kind that could not be reduced to an absurdity by applying it to one paint brush or box of pins. The general principle remains the same, and I would ask the minister to reply to my question.

I explained that we did not ask for tenders from any one but McAvity and Robertson, because the purchases were small and scattered, but the Department of Justice, when a large purchase is to be made, invites prices from the most reputable houses and the storekeeper is responsible in all cases for paying the lowest market price. The instructions are to take good care not to pay over the market price.
The answer is not satisfactory; where does he draw the arbitrary line between large and small purchases?

I suppose the answer my hon. friend wants is that we have a patronage list and will stick to it; then he could sail in and abuse us. If we were buying a hundred sacks of cement or a few barrels of flour we W'ould ask for prices-
By tender?
By circular from the best houses in the line. I see my friend smiling; that is what we do.
That is what you ought not to do.
No. If we followed your policy we would not do it, but we do it in spite of that. We ask all houses for prices
All houses?
All houses reputed to be good houses. We take the best houses in the line and ask prices and take the lowest price.

Take the Kingston penitentiary. Will the Solicitor General say that general tenders are asked for supplies from all reputable houses and that circulars are sent to them irrespective of their party politics?

In speaking of one hundred bags of cement I was simply using an illustration. The articles principally used in the penitentiaries are as follows, and before buying them we invite competition by public advertisement in the newspapers.
For a year's supply?

For a year's supply, the contract is for a year. The list is as follows:
Fresh meat, pork, bacon, coal, coal oil, cord-wood, milk, blankets and prison clothing, grocery staples, grocery sundries, sole leather, leather findings, hardware sundries, hardware staples, dry goods sundries, dry goods staples, oil, tinware, fish, drugs.
Next year we will add cement to this list.
Lumber?
We cannot specify in advance what lumber we will require.

That is satisfactory. I always had an idea that the Justice Department was kept pretty clear from the evils of the patronage system, but I began to get suspicious when I heard the answers of the Solicitor General. I understand it is intended to add other articles to the list next year and that the department will advertise and take the lowest tender. That is a perfectly intelligible and businesslike basis, and if that is the system adopted, I am very glad to know it and to know that it is being lived up to in that department. I would like to have from the First Minister a statement whether that is the system which is to be adopted by the government as a whole? The country is interested in this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it is the system which is followed in every department, but to be doubly sure I shall Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
reserve my answer until I make further inquiries, and I shall give the information the next time we go into Supply.
I would like to ask the minister who tendered for these dry goods, which he says were purchased by tender, and if samples were given to the different tenderers?

When tenders are called for, they are accompanied by a sample. The tenderers were: Lewis & Patterson, Montreal: P. Garneau, Fils & Cie., Quebec; Hodgson, Sumner & Co., Montreal; and A. Racine & Co., Montreal, who were the lowest.

My hon. friend must know that there are in Kingston some of the largest wholesale houses in Canada, and why were they not invited to tender? Why go to Montreal and pay larger prices than the goods could be purchased for in Kingston?

My hon. friend is under a misapprehension. These tenders were called for by advertisement in the newspapers. He does not expect us to go to Kingston and press his friends to tender. They had an equal opportunity to do so with the others, and every article mentioned in the Auditor General's Report was not bought on the schedule price given in the tender.
Will my hon. friend say in what newspapers the advertisement for these tenders appeared?
I have not the information, but can bring it down.
Was it published in any newspapers besides those of Montreal?
Certainly-in Kingston, St. John. Toronto, Montreal, Quebec and Halifax.
Is there a patronage list of newspapers?

I suppose my hon. friend would expect the department to consider the interests of this country and to advertise in papers having the largest circulation and most read by the people. Therefore he can draw his own conclusion.

In answer to that, I may say that last year I directed the government's attention to the fact that they had spent $600 in advertising for tenders for a small post office in a town in western Ontario, and the advertisement went into Reform newspapers only. I gave the circulation of the London ' Free Press,' in the very centre of that district, which has a larger circulation than any other newspaper, and strange to say, it was not on the patronage list.
It ought to be.
My hon. friend from Essex sees the importance of what I say.
Do I understand the hon. Solicitor General to say that lumber is not to be on the stock-list for future purchases?
Yes.

I think it should be, because I find on page L-17 of the Auditor General's Report that for hemlock $14 a thousand was paid to W. C. Edwards & Co., and $22.50 a thousand to the Fronte-nac Lumber & Coal Company, a difference of $8.50 a thousand.

The difficulty is that we cannot ask for any definite quantity of lumber as we can of flour or coal, because we do not know what kind or dimensions we may require during the year, and the quantity is not very great. I will try to find out the reason for the difference in price.

I would thank the hon. gentleman to bring down the schedule of prices of the different articles of dry goods in the tender of Messrs. Racine & Co.; because 1 am certain that Mclnnis & Co., of Kingston are prepared to compete with any house in Montreal if they had the opportunity.
Does my hon. friend think we used any means to prevent the Kingston people tendering? They were as much at liberty to tender as any others. I will bring the schedule of prices

The practice followed in every great city is to call for tenders for millions of feet of lumber before they know what thev want. They get the prices for dimension lumber and dressed lumber, so that if you want 10,000 or 20,000 feet of dimension lumber, you know exactly what you are going to pay for it.
The suggestion of my hon. friend is worth considering and we will see whether we can work it out or not.
Will the hon. minister give us the dimensions of the lumber he paid $52 per thousand for ?
I have not the information here.
We ought to have it.
I said I could not account for the discrepancy but no doubt it was due to the season or other conditions.
The worst feature is that you buy 1,000 feet at $14 and then you buy 10,000 feet at $22.50. There must be great discrepancy in the quality.
I am not an expert in lumber and cannot account for the difference in price. It may be due to difference in grades. I shall however get the information.
But a few minutes ago the minister said it was used for wharf repairs.
Yes, but I did not know the size of it.

It is well known that Georgian Bay district practically fixes the price for lumber, and those well posted know that mill run hemlock sold for $14 per 1,000 f.o.b. and that lumber from 16 feet to 18 feet was worth a dollar more, and over 18 feet, two dollars more. To these you would have to add the freight and the dealer's profit, so that the prices would be reasonable.
If you will come to Algoma we will give you the lumber at a good deal less than $14 per thousand feet.
Will the hon. gentleman say that the price of hemlock was the same then as to-day ?
You can get any amount at Algoma considerably under $14 per 1,000 feet.
Lumber is selling at four to five dollars a thousand feet less than a year ago.
As this is a discrepancy which the minister cannot understand, he might ask his officer to get the information and let us come back to the item again.
In view of the declaration by the minister that tenders were called for, how is it that we find several firms supplying similar goods at different prices ?
In the case of each penitentiary, we call for tenders.
I am quoting from page L-17 and 18 of the Auditor General's Report re Kingston penitentiary. Take James Crawford, Kingston.
He has the contract for supplying groceries.
But we also find groceries supplied by A. McLean, Kingston.
He supplied bacon and barley and pork.

He also supplied groceries. In dry goods, I find the same thing. I find dry goods bought from Hodgson, Sumner and Company, Montreal, and from Racine and Company, Montreal and from J. Tweeddell, Kingston.
Hodgson, Sumner and Company have the contract for sundry dry goods and Racine and Company for staples.

Take Dorchester penitentiary. F. M. Leblanc of Memramcook supplied 2,124 pounds of beef, at $5.87 per hundred-weight, and you paid Charles McKenzie, of Sackville, 7i cents per pound for 26,442 pounds of beef. I thought that in the case of beef, tenders would be invited for a year's supply, and I cannot understand this discrepancy.

Leblanc tendered at $5.87 per hundred-weight and supplied some beef at that price before signing the contract. Then he found he had tendered too low and refused to sign a contract, and we gave the contract to the next lowest tenderer.

The minister made the statement that Hodgson, Sumner and Company had the contract for sundry goods and Racine and Company for staples. How it is then that the same lines of goods are charged in both accounts ? In the one case 104 dozen shirts and drawers are paid for at $4.50 and in the other 12 dozen shirts and drawers are paid for at $4.75. He bought from Mr. Mills, his friend in Kingston, straw hats at $1.25, and from Hodgson and Sumner straw hats at $1.10. It would appear that the same kind of goods are divided up piecemeal between Hcdgson and Sumner and Racine and Company. If Mclnnis and Company of Kingston who are large wholesale men got an opportunity for tendering they would be able to supply these goods if they were not shuffled out of the contract.
Are they Conservatives?
They happen to be Tories.

Tenders are called for publicly through the press and everybody has an opportunity of competing. What my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) calls a discrepancy is explained by the fact that these goods are given to the convict when he is discharged from the penitentiary.
If I understand Mr. Taylor's contention it is that the patronage should be given to some one in the. city of Kingston.
All other things being equal.

If I am rightly informed there is only one wholesale house in Kingston, and therefore there would be no competition if tenders were invited only from firms in that city. Racine & Co. and Hodgson, Sumner & Co., of Montreal, are firms Mr. ARTHURS.
of high repute, and as I have some knowledge of the value of dry goods I can say that the goods are. supplied by these firms at fair prices.

I cannot understand why clothing supplied to the prisoners while serving their term is classed as staple articles and tenders called for in respect of same, while clothing supplied to all prisoners, when leaving the prison is not classed as staples and no competition asked in purchasing same.
I see by the Auditor General's Report that you paid $44 for street car tickets. Were these for the convicts?
The penitentiary is quite a distance from the city, and these tickets are given to officers who go to the city on official business.
Do all officers get them?
Only the accountant and storekeeper, and occasionally the engineer.
You have made a reduction of $40,000 in the binder twine item; what is the explanation of that?
That is because we are not buying any hemp this year. We have on hand 850,352 pounds of twine and 210,516 pounds of fibre.
What has been the average manufacture of twine for the past two or three years?
About 400,000 pounds a year.
Was more manufactured last year than usual?
The sales were not up to the average last year.
For what reason ? last year was a great wheat year.
We sent circulars last year as. usual to the Farmers' Associations, and to every one who had purchased from the department previously and we gave the same publicity as in former years.
Was the twine of inferior quality or was the outside competition greater?
The main reason is that we require cash with order, and all other manufacturers sell on time.
But you have always required the cash?
Money was scarcer last year than the year before, and as we required cash that may account for the difference.
Does the report of the department give that as a reason or is that mere theory?
The inspector informs me that there was a heavy demand made for binder twine last year if we would sell it on credit, but as we required cash they would not buy from us.

Do you purpose varying your method in future so as to sell on credit when you get sufficient guarantee? The twine industry was started at Kingston to give healthy employment to the inmates and is it not better to adopt a prudent credit system rather than let the industry die out, and leave the convicts without employment?

I am informed by the officer that shortly after the system was installed at Kingston, they sold some of the twine on credit, and they had any amount of trouble in collecting the money that was due for the twine. Perhaps the hon. member for Toronto may be able to suggest some better plan, but for the present we propose to continue on a cash basis.

I will suggest this plan to the Solicitor General. Some years ago the Minnesota State Binding Twine Institution found that they could not sell their twine for cash, and they had to take orders for twine from the farmers, on their note. Eight or ten farmers jointly signed a note for the twine they wanted for the year, each being responsible for the whole amount. As soon as the harvest was over and the grain was marketed, they had the money in hand to pay for these notes. I suggest to the department whether that plan might not be worth consideration, that eight or ten farmers should join together and each be responsible for the whole. I do not see that there would be any danger then. Before harvest very few farmers, in some parts of the country, have ready cash.

The minister stated a little while ago that a tender for staple dry goods was given to Messrs. Alphonse Racine & Co., and for sundries to Messrs. Hodgson, Sumner & Co. Turning to page L-17 it appears that he purchased lines of the same goods from Messrs. P. Garneau Fils & Co., of Quebec, for $1,545. In that order were shirts and drawers, 15 dozens at $4.50, 20 doz. at $6, and 20 doz. at $6.25. Other parties had tendered for supplying these goods, and yet the department go down to Quebec and give an order there for $1,545 without tender.

I am informed by the officer that in respect to shirts and drawers there was a shipment made by Garneau & Sons to. finish up a contract they had in the previous year, and it was paid out of the appropriation for this year.
Were potatoes considered a staple article of groceries for which tenders were called?
No. They grow their own potatoes at the penitentiary, and they buy only when they are short in their crops.

If there is anything of a staple character I should think it would be potatoes. But I find that you paid six different men for potatoes at varying prices. Would it not be better to advertise and get a price for potatoes for the year? Did you call for public tenders for flour?
Yes.

How is it, then, that flour is purchased from two or three different individuals at varying prices? You purchased flour from James Cummings, 410 barrels at $4.90; from Higham and Ramsay, Stonewall, Manitoba, you purchased 1,548 bags of flour at $1.80, and 410 bags at $2.45, less freight, $256. If the minister calls for tenders for flour at the lowest prices, how is it that he paid these varying prices?

Last year no tenders were called for and no contracts were given for flour. Generally we do call for tenders, but last year the market was so unsettled that the officers of the department thought it was better not to advertise for tenders, and they did not call for tenders. But that is only one year.
Do you call for tenders for molasses? I find molasses appearing in three different places. Molasses appears in the Crawford account and in the Maclean account, at different prices.
' Tenders were invited for this year and we have let contracts for the current year.
Were they invited last year?
Last year they were not invited, for the reasons I have stated.
Molasses appears in the Crawford account, 438 gallons at 35 cents, and in the Maclean account, 93 gallons at 36 cents. What is the explanation?

The Crawford account was under contract. In regard to the Maclean account, the officer explains that it may be an overlapping of the previous
year.
Is that all?
I do not know; I will have to find it out.

The minister might look at this item:	Brown sugar, 8,000 pounds,
at $3.85 per cwt., bought from Mr. Maclean. Surely brown sugar is a staple article, or was the market unstable there also ?

I am not in a position to give the explanation just now. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has asked for the schedules; I will bring them down and then my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) may satisfy himself.
The schedules will not satisfy one on that point.
You will see by the schedules what we got prices for and what the prices were.
If the tenders were accepted that is the man from whom the goods should have been purchased.
Certainly.
But they were not purchased from him.
They may have been classed as staples and sundries. One man might tender for grocery staples and the other for sundries.
Are these items staples or sundries?
I do not know.

I take from the list, potatoes, flour, molasses, beans, butter, barley; all these are purchased from different individuals. If these are not staples one would be at a loss to understand what staples are. Is there anything the minister considers a staple article of groceries which staple article he has purchased by tender from the lowest tenderer and from that man alone?
I stated just now that all these things are purchased from the lowest tenderer.
From that man alone?
There might be various contractors for the different institutions.
They may not be the lowest tenderers.
I admit I cannot explain this. When I get the schedules down we can again take up the matter and see why these things were purchased from two different parties.
The minister said that the flour market was unsettled last fall?
Not last fall, but a year ago last fall.
The price of wheat was pretty steady last fall.
Last October we had to ask for tenders, but it was a year ago last fall-October, 1907-that I had reference to.
That is just when the elections were on.
No.
You said you asked for tenders in October last?
Certainly we asked for tenders in October last, but we did not ask for tenders because the elections were on.
Last year wheat was very cheap and yet they paid $4.90 for flour.
I will have to retract. I am informed by the inspector that tenders were called for in the public newspapers after the elections.

That is explained in this way:	The year before there was a pretty
definite idea that there would be an election here; it was considered that the markets would be unsettled and, therefore, no tenders were asked for. Is that it ?
I would like to ask my hon. friend if there is any other kind of work done at the penitentiaries than the making of binder twine?

We make our own clothing, boots and shoes, and we work for other penitentiaries. We have in the penitentiaries eight instructors for the purpose of training convicts in various trades-carpenters, stonemasons, quarrymen, brick-makers, &e.
Do you make any shirts or drawers?
No, we buy them; we make pants and coats though.
Is there any of the product sold outside of the penitentiary?
No.
Or given away?

There is nothing given away. I am informed by the inspector that sometimes some of the goods manufactured by the convicts are sold outside. There are articles of furniture which are manufactured in the penitentiary for the officers and paid for by them. Of course, they are manufactured by the convicts, who are being taught their trade at the same time.

I think that if there are articles of furniture manufactured there and sold to the officers it might give rise to abuses. The case I referred to more particularly was this one:	A complaint was
sent to me about 96 church pews that had been manufactured at the penitentiary at St. Vincent de Paul, sent up from there to some church in Ottawa and sold for the sum of-I do not exactly remember the sum -but $100 or so. These pews were large and commodious, capable of accommodate

ing six people and were worth $960 at a low valuation. I would like to know exactly what occurred in regard to this transaction.

I am informed that there were some pews made by the convicts for a church at Ottawa. The lumber was supplied by the members of the congregation and the sum of $106 was paid for the labour which was used in making these pews by the convicts. That is the only instance.
Did the church put up an election subscription?
It was not that kind of church.
It put up the prayers.
Was the lumber sent down from Ottawa and through whom was that transaction carried out?

The lumber was sent down from Ottawa and the transaction was carried out through Mr. Dawson, inspector of penitentiaries. He thought it was a good thing to give our apprentices in the carpenter shop some work. The inspector gave them the lumber and saw that the cost of the labour that was put on this work was paid by the congregation.

Is Mr. Dawson at liberty to do that generally? There are a great many churches that would like to get pews at that rate. I think it is the most extraordinary transaction I have heard of in a long time.
I understand that this has been done on other occasions. One precedent is the supplying of cut stone for a church at Portsmouth, where Sir John Thompson paid the money and furnished the material.
Sir John Thompson had nothing to do with it.
He paid for the cut stone out of his own pocket.
After it was discovered that it had been furnished from the penitentiary.	_
I did not say when he paid it.
He said it should not have been done at the expense of the people of Canada, and he paid for it out of his own pocket when he found the work had been done at the penitentiary
It was not paid for in this case by the people of Canada; the $106 did not come from the people of Canada, but from the congregation.

That is not exactly the point of view to take. The question is, what kind of operations can be carried on 29J
in a general way. My hon. friend knows that there is serious conflict between prison and outside labour, and if this sort of thing can be done in one instance why can it not in another? My information is that at the penitentiary I have mentioned there are serious disorders of that kind. As I have no precise facts that I can establish I do not wish to refer to those disorders in a general way, but this particular case goes to show that the inspector has the right to order work to be done for outside parties for remuneration in money, and I think that is at least opening the door to very serious abuse. It is not fair. If our convicts in the penitentiary can be employed, for instance, on public works, there is a great deal of work that can be done without their labour competing with that of outsiders. That competition we should not encourage. It cannot be allowed to take place.

The inspector has just explained to me that the work was done at his request for himself; he says it was his contribution to the church I take issue with my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) when he says that at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary there are disorders of that kind. I want to register a protest. Last year he made charges against the officers and administration of the penitentiary. I spent a week there and made the most minute investigation, but found there was no foundation for the charges made against the officials there.
What are the charges against which he protests?
You say there is great disorder in that line in that penitentiary.
When did you hold an investigation?
Last year after, you and the then member for Laval made your charges against the warden and officials of the penitentiary

I find it extremely singular that the Solicitor General should have held an investigation there of charges I made without giving me an opportunity of appearing before His Worship to establish the charges. I do not think the investigation was of a very serious character. The only charge I made was that the prefect of the penitentiary took an active, open and violent part in elections. If the Solicitor General went down there and found that the prefect took no part in the elections I cannot say that I think much of his investigation, because it is well known there that Mr. Beauchamp took a very violent part in every election in that county since 1896. That was the only charge I made at that time, but I am making another one

now. My hon. friend seems to become terribly indignant because we offered criticism-
Not at all.

What are we here for, to burn incense before my hon. friend?
Mr. BUREAU I wish you would.

I thought we were called upon to point out defects to criticise, and I say that I have had reports that the inspection is not properly done there, that work is done, articles are manufactured there and taken out of the penitentiary.
And paid for.

No, but I have no other instance, but that one about which there is no doubt whatever. An order was given for the manufacture of furniture, worth $960, for which $104 was paid. I take the view that it is unfair; if you open the door to that kind of thing you could have a furniture manufacturer getting furniture manufactured there, you can have prison labour in opposition to free labour. My hon. friend need not get indignant. We on this side of the House will not stand for protest and indignation because we offer fair criticism and bring facts to the notice of the government.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER The item before the committee deals with Kingston penitentiary; shall this carry?

Yes, but upon that item I raised the question of penitentiary labour. If I am out of order I will abide by your ruling, but I think that in voting $50,000 for Kingston penitentiary, I am at liberty to raise the question of prison labour.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Two questions have been brought up. The last point is a reasonable one and I think might come under this item, whether or not it is proper and advisable that prison labour should be sold outside of the penitentiary. That is a very old question of debate in this House. But there was another the hon. member (Mr. Monk) did not exactly state, but he insinuated that something had been done which was not absolutely correct, that these pews had been sold to the congregation at a lower price than their real value. As I followed the discussion I think he is satisfied that there has been no dishonesty and nothing wrong whatever, whatever the wisdom of the policy might be. As I understand, the material was furnished by the congregation and the labour, which was supplied by the penitentiary, was paid for by the congregation. Under such circumstances it seems to me there is nothing wrong and that matter should more properly come up when we are discussing the votes for St.

Vincent de Paul penitentiary. In the meantime my hon. friend has suggested a larger question whether or not the labour of the convict should be permitted to compete with the ordinary labour. That is a question which has been discussed again and again in this House for the last thirty years. I do not know that anything has been done to assert a principle one way or the other. Generally it was supposed that the labour of the convict should not come in competition with free labour and if this is the only instance, it seems to me to be not worth while discussing it.

That is true to a certain extent; I think both governments have gone on the principle of not allowing the convict labour to come in competition with ordinary labour. It seemed to be felt that some useful and steady employment could be found for the prisoners, and the compromise was the establishment a good many years ago of the binder twine manufactory which has been carried on ever since in Kingston. But that is different from a general policy announced by this government of not coming into competition with the general labour of the country. That is different from the general policy which has actuated both governments, of not allowing prison labour to enter into competition with the general industries and employments of the country. I do not agree with my hon. friend, however, in treating this matter so cavalierly. I think it is not only unwise, but wrong. I would like to ask whether the department authorized this particular instance or not. It was asserted by my hon. friend that Sir John Thompson had done the same. Will he make the statement in this House that Sir John Thompson, as Minister of Justice, or as premier, authorized that to be done ? Or, was it not a matter which, when found out, was not approved of by Sir John Thompson, who took as manly a way as he possibly could of getting out of it ? But I think you go a long way into competition with the ordinary trades and labour of the country when you allow the inspector of penitentiaries to furnish a church with $900 worth of furniture for $104.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not a fair way of putting it.
I understand that pews which were worth about $900 were got by the church.
They furnished the lumber.

I know. The church produced the lumber for making the pews and got the labour for almost nothing. If they had to go into the general market and thus had given employment to the trades in that

line, they would have paid a great deal more, and the trades would have got the advantage. In this case, while the whole country is keeping up the penitentiary, this one particular church gets that advantage. I do not think that ought to be allowed, and I would like to hear whether or not the minister of the department gave his authority for that transaction.

The minister never gave any special authority to the inspectors. The inspectors took it upon themselves to do this. While on my feet, I may correct an error of the hon. member for North Toronto, who is under the impression that 96 pews were furnished. There were only 42. The lumber was sent to St. Vincent de Paul, and the time was put in by the convicts. It is true, the whole country supports the convicts, and if any churcn gets the advantage of the cheap labour, every other church should have the same; but still this was a special case. The worthy inspector tells me that it was done in perfect good faith.

I do not know what church is in question, and I have no doubt that the object for which these pews were ordered was an excellent one; but I object to the principle. I put a question on the subject to the House the other day, and I believe the answer was that there were 63 pews. Now the number Is stated to have been 42. The information sent to me was that there were 96, the value of which was $960. If you open the door to that kind of thing, it means the employment of prison labour to the detriment of outside labour; and I believe that both governments have agreed that that should not be done. In that letter there was an insinuation, as my right hon. friend says, that this was more or less of a practice at St. Vincent de Paul. If so, I think it is important that it should be put a stop to. In connection with Kingston penitentiary I find that there was a revenue of $10,646.93 outside of the binder twine industry. The farm contributed $3,402.41, the tailor $2,579.20, stone $598, and so on. Was this revenue derived from sales made outside, or what is the nature of it ?

; While the hon. Solicitor General is looking up the answer, I wish to make one statement in justice to the memory of Sir John Thompson. As soon as he found out that those articles were purchased from the penitentiary, he instituted an inquiry, the result of which was that condign punishment was inflicted upon the subordinate officers who caused the transfer of the work from the penitentiary to the church authorities, and he saw that the country did not suffer to the extent of one dollar by paying the money himself.

The revenue from the bakery represents bread sold to the officers; that from the blacksmiths' shop represents
work done for other penitentiaries; that from the tailor represents contracts executed by the penitentiary for the Department of Indian Affairs and the Department of the Interior. That is the largest amount.
Is any of it from work done for outside parties ?
No.
I understand that this was done by the inspector on his own mere motion. Is' it part of the inspector's duty or right to make contracts with outsiders for prison labour ?
The inspector, as I said just now, gave the work himself. The inspector gave out the work himself.
To what church does he belong?

St. Matthew's. Is that my hon. friend's church? The lumber was sent in to the inspector, and he ordered the work to be done as if it were for himself. Being a member of that church, that was his contribution. The time was kept of the labour making the pews, and he paid for that labour at the rate charged for penitentiary work.
He did that as an officer?
Yes, and I do not want my hon. friend to understand that I approve of the policy. It is one that is open to question.
I would think that an inspector of penitentiaries has certain duties to perform, and that outside of these he has no authority to become a contractor for churches or any one else.

That is hardly putting the case fairly. It has always been the custom for penitentiary officers to have their furniture made by the convicts, and they pay the usual penitentiary rates. This gives employment to the convicts. The inspector did not act as a contractor but as a member of the church, and he availed himself of his privilege as an officer of the penitentiary to have work done for the church as he would for himself, paying the same rates. It was done for a good purpose, and the country lost nothing, and on the question of putting an end to that question I am not ready to pronounce.

I should have hoped that my hon. friend would have been ready to say no and say it at once. This case arises out of the fact that you give to your officers a perquisite in that way, and that leads us back to the consideration whether an officer should have any perquisites of that kind at all. Why should any officer have the right to get his furniture cheaper than an outsider? The country is paying him a proner

salary or it ought to do so; and this is one of the perquisites, many of which were abolished, and I do not know why this one was allowed to remain.
How will you keep your convicts busy?

You should not say that in order to keep them busy, you will allow perquisites to your officers. There are other ways of keeping your convicts occupied. Pay each officer his wage and eive him no favours. I would ask the leader of the House what estimates will be taken up after six o'clock? We are at a loss by not knowing five minutes ahead what is to be gone on with. That makes it more difficult for us and the ministers as well. If we knew a day in advance, we would be better prepared to facilitate the business, and the minister himself might be prepared to expedite it if he would only take counsel with his officers before he comes to the House.
What ought to be going on to-day is the work of the Opposition, but instead they allow their motions to stand on the order papers, and then expect the government to take up its business.
What will we go on with to-night?
With these penitentiary estimates.
And what after?

I am glad to hear my hon. friend give indication of such diligence in expediting business. We shall, probably, go on with the Indian estimates and Interior Department.
At six o'clock House took recess.
After Eecess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I find that the department paid {3.60 per barrel for 724 barrels of flour purchased from Higham & Ramsay, of Stonewall, and that the department also purchased from a man named Cummings 410 barrels of flour at $4.90 per barrel. What is the reason for this great difference in the price. Every one knows that the flour made in Manitoba is the best flour in the world, and no better flour can be found any where than that made in the Stonewall mills in my constituency. How did you come to p>ay Mr. Cummings $4.90 when you only paid $3.60 to Messrs. Higham & Ramsay? While on my feet I may say that I was rather surprised at the statement of the Solicitor General to the effect that the question of employing convict labour in competition with free labour was open to discussion. I believe that every member in this House will agree Mr. FOSTER.
with me that the principle of allowing convicts to make $900 worth of pews for a church at a cost of some $120 is a wrong principle. It brings convict labour into direct competition with free labour and it should not be tolerated. The Solicitor General, in what I consider a rather flippant manner, said that he did not endorse the principle but he thought it was open for discussion. I say that it is not open for discussion; it is absolutely a wrong principle.

The hon. gentleman ought not to say that pews worth $900 were furnished for $120. I do not say that the principle is right, but it is only fair to say that the parties who got the pews furnished their own lumber.
That does not alter the principle at all.
It alters the fact.

There is no doubt whatever that the pews were made by convict labour and furnished at a much less cost than if they were made by free labour. It is the old story of convict labour coming into competition with free labour and the principle is wrong.

I do not say that the principle is right in this particular case, and while I do not want convict labour to come into competition with free labour, yet, these prisoners are learning a trade and it is rather difficult sometimes to draw the line. The officers of the penitentiary are allowred to have certain articles made by convict labour and they pay for them.
Does the Solicitor General approve of that system?
I did not say that I did. but the question having been raised I said it was worth considering.
What about that difference in the price paid for the flour?
I am informed that the price of flour varied last year and that the current market price was paid at the time the flour was purchased.
My hon. friend from Selkirk may not be aware that Mr. Cummings who got the high price for the flour was the Liberal candidate in Brockville some time ago.
That would not make any difference. Does the hon. gentleman say that more than the current market price was paid?

How is it that if, as we are told, tenders were called for staple articles and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer and the goods purchased

from him, that these same staple goods have been purchased from so many different parties.
That was in the case of molasses and sugar.

The explanation given by the Solicitor General was that potatoes were not purchased by tender because it was only when more potatoes than were grown on the penitentiary grounds were required that potatoes were ^purchased; but as some 1,500 barrels were purchased during the year surely the department cou'd have made a nearer estimate as to its requirements than that. The Solicitor General told us that as the price of flour fluctuated last year tenders were not called for, but he gave us no explanation with regard to the prices paid for molasses, and barley, and beans, and cheese, and butter. Is the minister prepared' to give that information now?
The officers leave the department at six o'clock and any how I had not time to go there.
We can rely on getting that information to-morrow?
Yes.
Will we get the information before these estimates are passed?
We can do it on some other item. I will leave an item open.
I understood the minister to say that they considered it inadvisable to sell twine to the farmers on credit. Can he tell me what was the length of credit, as a rule, asked by the farmers?
They asked until after the harvest to pay for the twine, those who asked for credit.
Is it not a fact that in the case of Higham and Ramsay they actually tendered for that flour? Were tenders called for in any other case?

I have explained this afternoon that we did not invite tenders a year ago on account of the unsettled condition of the flour market. These gentlemen had been supplying the penitentiaries before, and we bought from them They were a reliable firm who had been doing business with us before.

' I understood the minister to say that the officials of the penitentiary were allowed to purchase things that were made in the penitentiary, such as furniture. I see a large amount of revenue here derived from the tailor. Are the officials entitled to get anything in the shape of clothes, or anything from the shoemaker's shop?

They get clothing and shoes for their families and themselves. The greater part of the revenue from the tailor is owing to the fact that we take contracts with the Indian Department; all the tailor work required on the Indian reservation is done in the penitentiary at Kingston, and we charge it up against the Indian Department.
On what basis is the price fixed for these goods, and who fixes the price?

The price is fixed by the accountant of the penitentiary, and by the instructor of the particular branch in which the work is done, upon the basis of 30 cents for labour, the cost of material, and also the cost of supervision.

Turning to L-18,
I find that you purchased from Geo. E. May-bee, of Napanee, castile laundry soap, 2,114 lbs. at 5 cents. Who is Mr. Maybee?
Mr. Maybee is a manufacturer's agent.
The hon. gentleman is misinformed. Mr. Maybee is a commercial traveller who visits our town, and I have known him for many years.
He represented himself to us as a manufacturer's agent.
Who would be responsible for buying supplies that were not advertised for by tender for the penitentiaries?

In such a case a requisition is made by the storekeeper^ then it is handed over to the warden, and if the warden approves of it, he turns it over to the inspectors, and if they approve, the purchase is made. Of course it goes before the minister.

I see that 1,700 bushels of potatoes were bought in that way. For some, 60 cents a bushel were paid; for others, $1 a bushel, to the same man. No doubt if a staple like that had been advertised for you would have got the whole quantity for 60 cents a bushel.
That might be, but we could not take delivery of the whole quantity at once. These were bought at different times when the prices varied.

Could the minister give us a detailed statement showing how much of this revenue was derived from the sales of goods, altogether apart from the government and the penitentiary; also, showing what proportion of it is sold to the officials?

I could get that information, but it would take some time to prepare it. I would suggest that the hon. gentleman put a motion on the order paper

for a return. It would give us a better chance to get the whole of the details out.
Were tenders called for the sand that was supplied?
No.

That does not give the information. The question which has been asked is this: Is it the intention to purchase these articles, where they are obtained in large quantities, by tender or by private advices to men in the business?
I would like to know whether or not you grow your own potatoes at the penitentiary in Manitoba and whether you are carrying on the farming industry in connection with that institution?
We try to grow them.
Does the minister mean to insinuate that we cannot grow potatoes in Manitoba? If they made an attempt at all there is no doubt that they would succeed in growing them.
We did grow them, too.
I would like to know whether or not they have been able to supply the demand there or did you go out in the open market to purchase them?
There were no potatoe purchased in Manitoba, as appears by th details of the penitentiary report, page 168 I hey were all grown there.

The reason I asked th. question a few minutes ago as to the pur chasing of sand for the penitentiary is this In the county of Frontenac there are threi persons engaged in the sand business. Twi ot these are strong Liberals and the othe: one is a strong Conservative. In gettim sand for the Rockwood asylum, which i: under the provincial government, tender: are asked for and the two Liberals have ar equal chance with the Conservative to sup ply that sand. But in getting sand for tin penitentiary apparently tenders are no asked for and a fair chance is not giver to all parties. I hope this system will b< changed in the future in fairness to al persons engaged in this business.
Carried.
I think my hon. friend is entitled to an answer as to whether sane will be purchased by tender.
He expressed a hope: Wc do not know the quantity of sand that wc will require.
You required in the neighbourhood of 200 cubic yards last year.
This seems an unreasonable evasion. You must be buying sand in large quantities in future. The question is whether it will be bought by tender.
We only bought $189 worth.

The Conservative that I referred to and who is engaged in the sand business has been distinctly told on more than one occasion that there was no need of him tendering or thinking of supplying sand to the Kingston penitentiary because of his politics, and I am asking if that sort of thing is going to be allowed, or if you are going to give everybody a fair show as is done ip buying sand for the Rockwood asylum?

I think it is only fair to know by whom the hon. gentleman was told that. If any officials said that to the hon. gentleman's friend they certainly ought to be reprimanded. It might have been told to the hon. gentleman by one of his political friends for the purpose of using it in the House for all I know.
In our portion of the country we do not consider that reprimands would do much good. In election time these officials go out and work as actively as any person in the county.
Does the reprimand you speak of mean an advance in salary?

As a Canadian manufacturer I have an important question to ask. By reference to page L-18 of the Auditor General's Report I find that there were 88 hats bought from a Canadian firm at $1 each. Turning to page L-17 of the Auditor General's Report I find that there were six dozen hats bought from Hicks & Son, London, England, at $1.25 each. As a manufacturer of Canada I would like to know if Canadian manufactured hats are not good enough for those penitentiary chaps at Kingston?
I am told that the hats that were bought in England were for the officers, being portions of their uniforms.
It does not say so in the Auditor General's Report. Even if they were, why could not they have been manufactured and purchased in Canada?
In the minister's report the whole thing is stated.
Might I ask for an expression of opinion in regard to the purchase of sand for the Kingston penitentiary? Is it to be done by tender or not?
We will be glad to ask the hon. gentleman's friend for a tender if he will give us his name.
I am young at this business, but I do not think that is an answer to my question.
Yes, I think it is. The hon. gentleman wants to find out whether we are going to purchase from the same party without inviting tenders
Whether by tender or by private agreement.
We are going to ask for prices.
I will be satisfied if the hon. gentleman will give me the assurance that when they want sand they will ask for tenders.

My hon. friend does not mean to say that if we want a load of sand w'e are going to advertise for it. If my hon. friend will give us his friend's name wo will send him .a circular and ask him for prices.

That is begging the question. You bought during the past year a large quantity of sand, and it is likely that you will buy a large quantity in the future. The question of the hon. gentleman is: Is it the intention of the government to buy by public tender or by contract with private individuals? He is entitled to an answer to that question.
It is not the intention to buy by private agreement with private parties.

At page L-36 of the Auditor General's Report, under the heading ' Twine returned into stock,' I see 88,260 pounds, valued at $10,149.90 and 24,050 pounds valued at $2,654.50 put down as having been returned. May I ask the minister if this twine was sold, found unsatisfactory and returned to the department?

The Canadian Society of Equity were overstocked, they had 88,260 pounds left on their hands and asked us to take the twine back; we did so and refunded them the money. The same thing applied to the 24,000 pounds.
Where is this firm ?

It is not a firm, it is an association of farmers in Alberta, for the whole province of Alberta. They club together and give their order but they had this on their hands after the crop was in and asked the authorities to take it back.
Was the freight paid on it to the penitentiary ?
It was taken to the penitentiary at Edmonton and is stored there.

My hon. friend is mistaken. In the next item he will find that
the Alberta Farmers' Association returned only 7,200 pounds. The minister should be careful and read the documents in his hands and give answers in accordance with the facts. The facts in this case are that some society of equity returned over 112,000 pounds but the Alberta Farmers Association returned only 7,200 pounds.

I am informed that the Canadian Society of Equity is an association in southern Alberta but the_ Alberta Farmers Association operates principally around Edmonton.
St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, $114,000.
The farmers will be glad to know that they pay $1.50 a bushel for barley, and $2.50 for peas down there.
I am informed that this grain was for seed.
How many bushels ?
25 bushels.
They paid $5.30 for flour to the Campbell Milling Company but at the next page I see tney got Manitoba hard at $3.60.

The market was fluctuating at that time. That year the flour market was very variable and it was decided not to advertise for tenders but to buy from time to time as we required it. That is the only year tenders were not asked for.
I see that a saddle horse was purchased from Alfred Charbon-neau for $245, a generous price.

We have a certain number of horses there, some for the farm and others for the mounted patrol. My hon. friend will admit that the patrol must have good horses if they are to be of any use. If a prisoner should escape on one of the farm horses the patrol could not overtake him unless he had a better horse.
Were the turnips for which you paid $1.10 a bushel for seed?
I suppose they were bought when the price of turnips was high or they might have been larger turnips.
I see that Robert R. Creighton a clerk at Ottawa was paid $232.79 for two trips Ottawa to Montreal and return.
That charge is right. Mr. Creighton was paid that amount. He is the accountant of the branch and wTas making an audit of the books, and that is for his travelling expenses.

I see at L-21 a purchase :
Kinsey Boyden, Cincinnati, Ohio, 9 ply jail bars 23,184 pounds at 8j cents, 24,185 pounds at 8i cents, 1,182 pounds at 9 cents.

Could these bars not be got in Canada?
I am informed that this steel bar, which is tool proof, is not made in Canada.
I would like to draw the attention of the Solicitor General to the fact that the Nova Scotia Coal and Steel Company roll steel bars of any shape and dimensions.
Do they roll tool proof steel in Nova Scotia?

I do not think they do.
Mr. BUREAU I may inform the hon. gentleman that there were inquiries made before it was bought to ascertain whether or not it was manufactured in Canada, and it was found that it was not.

I notice at page L-22 that spur gears were bought from the Platt Iron works Co., of Dayton, Ohio. I would like to ask the Solicitor General if it is the policy of the government to buy these things outside of the country when they can be bought in the country?
These were duplicate parts of a machine which came from there, and therefore they had to be obtained there.

The hon. gentleman was good enough to give us a list of the goods supplied to the Kingston penitentiary on public advertisement. Will he give us a list of the goods supplied to this penitentiary? For example, is coal supplied by tender?

Yes, it is. There were
two tenders-the T. F. Moore Co. and Cohen & Son. The tenders were called for by public advertisement in the newspapers.
Why was it that the price of coal in Montreal was over a dollar a ton more than it was in Kingston-the same grade of coal?
I cannot account for that. When we advertise in the newspapers for tenders, all we can do is to accept the lowest tender, which we have done.
What newspapers?
I have not got the list here. I will bring it down.
If the hon. gentleman will turn to page L-22, he will find that Alphonse Racine & Co. furnished goods. I want to know if they tendered for supplies there, and if so, what supplies?
There were tenders called for frieze, and theirs was the lowest tender. There were seven tenders put in.

They supplied shirts and drawers, 127 pairs, at $4.50 per Mr. BRADBURY.
pair, whereas at the Kingston penitentiary the price was $4.50 a dozen. Surely there is a rake-off there.
That is a printer's mistake. The word 'dozen' is omitted before the word 'pairs.' It should be 127 dozen pairs, at $4.50 a dozen.

At page L-21 there is an item of $2,173 for lumber, which ranges all the way from $20 to $55 a thousand. Will the minister kindly tell us what kind of lumber was bought at $55 a thousand, and was it bought by tender?
I have not the details of that item, but I will get them from the department and bring them down.

With reference to this coal purchase from L. Cohen & Son, will the minister tell me what quantity of coal was asked for in the advertisement, and did it specify screenings; also what were the names of the parties who tendered, and the prices of the tenders per ton.
The tender of Cohen & Son is for soft screenings at $3.75 a ton. 1,500 tons were asked for. The other tender, that of Moore & Co., of Montreal, was at $4.75 a ton.
When was the advertisement for tenders published ?
The supplies of the year 1907-8 were advertised to be tendered for up to March 18, for the various penitentiaries.
And only two tenders were received.
Yes.
Were the parties invited to tender for all the penitentiaries ?

It was optional for them to tender for one or for all the penitentiaries.
Dorchester penitentiary, $70,000.
Does the department still buy its hardware from the firm of Mc-Avity & Sons, of St. John, New Brunswick?
Lewis Brothers of Montreal are the contractors for the hardware, both sundries and staples, for the year 1907-8.
In the Auditor General's Report, I notice that upwards of $1,000 of hardware was purchased from McAvity & Sons.
These were plumber's' supplies and steam fittings, small orders given at different times, when the things were wanted quickly.

Without public tender or competition. Is the Solicitor General

aware that the head of this firm is George McAvity, the gentleman who got away with a rake-off of $35,900 in connection with the Mayes contract ? If that firm has any account against the government^ it might be well to set it off, so far as it will go, against that rake-off, seeing that the department is unwilling to take proceedings to recover back the $35,900. In connection with McAvity & Sons, I find that they received $2.45 per barrel for 120 barrels of Portland cement, but I notice that cement was purchased for the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary at $1.85. It might be interesting to the Department of Justice to know that the Public Accounts Committee of New Brunswick had occasion to investigate the accounts of McAvity & Sons some years ago when the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) was in the government of that province, and it was found that they were charging two prices in many instances.

The penitentiary at St. Vincent de Paul is right close to the market where they deal in cement, which may account for its being cheaper there. I do not know if there are any cement factories in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, and the difference in freight may explain the discrepancy. If you buy from Hull, you will have to pay more freight.
Would the freight account cause such a difference?
The purchase may have been at different times and larger quantities may have been required for St. Vincent de Paul than for Dorchester penitentiary.
I find that 235 barrels of Portland cement were bought from J. H. Hickman at $2.45.
Yes, the same price as from McAvity & Co.
The chaplain at this penitentiary receives $200 a year less than at St. Vincent de Paul. Is that by reason of his inferior capacity or less onerous duties?
Less onerous duties, on account of the population being less in Dorchester than in St. Vincent de Paul.

I find on page L-22 of the Auditor General's Report that the government purchased from T. Prefontaine & Co., Montreal, lumber commencing at $20 and running up to $75 per 1,000 feet. Unless this lumber was made into mahogany chairs or things of that kind, the price seems a fabulous one.
The $75 per 1,000 feet was paid for oak.

Could the minister say how much of the items for salaries
and retiring allowances at St. Vincent de Paul and Dorchester penitentiaries is for each separately ?
Last year there were $38,606.48 for salaries and $2,077.76 for retiring allowances.
The retiring allowances ought to be put separately in the estimates so that we might know them.
We cannot tell in advance what the retiring allowances for the year will be.
How many convicts in Dorchester penitentiary?
245, an excess of 51 over the previous year.
Were tenders called for the installation of a power plant at Dorchester?
We have no power plant; we are buying the electricity.
Was an estimate made of what it would cost to run your own power plant?
It was estimated that a plant would cost $10,000 and salaries of officers to run the plant $3,500 a year.
The Sackville Hay & Feed Company were paid $6.10 per barrel for some flour; $3.15 for other flour, and $4.85 per barrel for other flour. What is the explanation?

They were different grades of flour which were mixed together so as to lessen the cost.
Manitoba penitentiary, $60,350.

I notice by the Auditor General's Report that Scott & Stratton, of Stonewall, were paid $4,652 for various lumber supplies. Were these supplies bought by tender? Does the Solicitor General know that this is a very small firm doing business at Stonewall? Where there is such a lar-e amount of lumber required would it not be cheaper for the department to buy from a wholesale house in Winnipeg rather than from these small dealers?
I am informed the purchase was made after inviting prices. They tried to get the same goods in Winnipeg but they found they could not get as good service.

That explanation is hardly in line with what are the facts. Stonewall is about 8 miles from Stoney Mountain and Stoney Mountain is about the same distance from Winnipeg. There is a first-class train service from Winnipeg to Stoney Mountain, so that if the lumber were bought in Winnipeg it could -be delivered much easier at Stoney Moun-

tain than from Stonewall. There is something wrong in that explanation.
I am informed this firm took the order and shipped to Stoney Mountain. The inspector tells me he does not know where the lumber came from.
Were public tenders asked for, or was the contract simply given to these people?
Prices were invited from these people and from parties in Winnipeg, and the prices of these people were lower than the prices we got from Winnipeg.

Don't you see at once that when you invite tenders from only two or three people you leave room for that collusion which must have taken place in this case. A firm doing business like Scott & btratton, m Stonewall, could not sell as cheaply as a large firm in Winnipeg. A small firm like that outside of Winnipeg would have to buy from the Winnipeg firm, and resell it at a higher price to the government.	[DOT]
What firms were asked to tender for these supplies?

I have not that information. The prices were asked by the penitentiary officials.
Mr. GEORGE TAYLOR, that information?
You will get

I do not know. It is ask-inS a good deal of the officials to send us down copies of all their letters. They were instructed by the inspectors to ask for prices, and give the contract to the lowest tenderer.
Were their instruc tion given from Ottawa?
Yes.

You will bring down the instruction that was sent by the inspector who to buy it from.
Mr BUREAU There is a standing induction to all the purchasing agents of the various penitentiaries that they are to buy at the lowest market price.

I do not suppose the hon gentleman knows who the firm of Stratton & Scott are. Stratton is the president of the Liberal association of the

Does my hon. friend claim the prices are excessive?
I think they are in some cases.
I find an item of $48.40 for advertising for tenders for supplies. Was a tender asked for dry goods, and was the lowest tender accepted?
Yes.
Who was the lowest tenderer?

For dry goods special. J. M. Garland Sons & Co., of Ottawa. They received the contract for all the articles that are mentioned under the heading of dry goods special for all the penitentiaries in Canada. Dry goods staples for Manitoba went to Racine & Co.; there were four tenderers.

How do independent tenderers know that they may procure contracts? Unless the tenders are taken and accepted only as advertised, and for the articles advertised, then tendering is of no use to the country.

I think my hon. friend does not understand the matter correctly. If he would read the advertisement carefully he would see that in a general way it calls for tenders for certain supplies, with a form of tendering, and stating that particulars can be obtained on application to the warden. Then if he looks over the tender form, that would specify in detail the different kinds of groceries, and the different kinds of clothing, and so forth, required. One tenderer may be lower for one kind of clothing, and another lower for another kind, and that accounts for the contracts being given to different parties and not all to one.

There is no mention of that in the advertisement. The advertisement says that parties may tender for one or for all of the different public institutions, but it does not say that parties may tender for part of the dry goods, or for part of the groceries, or for anything else under any one heading. It simply invites tenders for one institution or for all. Consequently the public in general would not know that they could go to the department and divide up the tenders for part of the dry goods or part of the groceries; there is no hint of it in the advertisement. I think I understand the advertisement as well as the hon. gentleman.

If my hon. friend would refer again to the advertisement he will find that it states: ' Forms of tenders can be obtained, with particulars, from the warden '. Has my hon. friend ever seen one of these tender forms? Take a tender for different kinds of clothing for instance. One tenderer puts in a certain price for one class of goods, and another tenderer puts in a price for another class of goods, and so on. A third tenderer may be lower on one class of goods, and higher on another, and the department in each case gives it to the lowest tenderer for the particular kind of goods that is on the list. There is no patronage in the matter at all.

The specification is contained in the blank form of tender. By applying to the warden of the penitentiary he who desires to tender gets a form, and on that form every article is mentioned under a special heading.
