Here, for instance, is a tender for dry goods special, enumerating particulars of weight, colour and quality. They put their prices on the different articles. One may tender for blankets, another for prison clothing. The specification is on the tender. They apply for this from the warden, and they get an enumeration of all the various articles required under the special heading.
The minister can accept the tender as to one item, and reject it as to another. Is that not so?

In the form of the contract they say that samples or tenders will be considered item by item. Suppose a man is lower on blankets we will award him the contract for blankets and not for other things upon which he may not be as low.
I am afraid my hon. friend is neglecting the spiritual welfare of some of the inmates of this institution.
Where?-in Manitoba?
Yes. I see there are five chaplains who receive $688 and one who gets $1,000.
What page?
L-26. I would like to know if these five were all in service at the time or whether they were serving periodically, turn about?
They were serving periodically, turn about.

I would like to direct the attention of the hon. gentleman to page L-27.
Higham & Ramsay, Stonewall: bran, 1 Ion $18; Imperial flour, 620 bags at $1.55; sundry items, $3.90, $982.90.
A while ago the hon. gentleman stated that the tenders were called for after the general elections. If my memory serves me aright the contract was let for this flour in Selkirk about ten days or two weeks before the elections.
I am informed that the tenders were called for in November and the contract let in the same month.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he would bring the tender down, because this is a disputed point. It is in my own constituency, and I happen to know the circumstances. I am not complaining of Higham & Ramsay getting the contract because they happen
to be friends of my own, although my opponent was bidding high to get them as the public accounts will show. Two weeks before the election Higham & Ramsay received some assurance that if they had not obtained the contract they were going to obtain it. I would like to know whether that is a fact, and I would like the hon. gentleman to bring down the tender.
What about Stony Mountain?
It was sent in on title 26th November, 1908.
What is the date of the tender?
There is no date on the tender, but here is the letter transmitting the tender.
Is that the tender for the supply of flour for the Stony Mountain Penitentiary?
Yes.
What is the date of the tender?
The 26tli November, 1908.
Who is the tender addressed to?
The Inspector of Penitentiaries, Ottawa.
Who is it mailed by?
I have not the name of the office boy, but it was signed by the tenderers.
Who signed the tender?
The Ogilvie Flour Mills Co., Ltd., by R. Dobell.
What about the tender of Higham & Ramsay? That is the one I am asking for.
It is here. It is with the others that were put on the list in the month of November and the contract was awarded, I am told, in the beginning of December. Do you want to see it?

That is satisfactory;
I will take your word for it.
Are these tenders ever dated?
It all depends upon the man who fills it up. These are not dated. They generally inclose their tenders with a letter.

At page L-28 I see that Windatt & Co., Winnipeg, supplied 79-7 tons of coal at $9.20. The quality is not specified. Would the hon. gentleman tell us what the quality was and if it was bought by tender?
Yes, that coal was bought by tender after public advertisement. It was egg coal.

The tender sent over here looks all right, but there is no signature and no date. This only confirms the suspicion I have that this was all arranged before my election because it was street talk two weeks before the election that Higham & Ramsay had the contract to furnish the flour.

My hon. friend will understand we could not let the contract before we had the figures. They were the lowest tenderers. We have accompanying letters showing that they were mailed on the 26th and the 24th of November.
Does that not show the time they were transmitted to Ottawa?

Here is the Campbell Milling Company tender dated November 28 and not signed. Here is the tender of Cum-ming, of Lynn Lin, dated November 28. All these people were on the list and the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer. All these being on the list there could not be any game, because we did not know who was the lowest tenderer.

I am quite satisfied to take the hon. gentleman's word for it, but it looked peculiar.
There is an allowance to school district 294, Stony Mountain, in lieu of school fees of $250. It is a great hardship to the residents of that district to have this amount so small; the government should allow that district at least $500. The settlement is very small; they have kept up the school; the larger number of pupils attending it are children of the officials, and the government are not bearing their fair share of the burden.

The matter deserves consideration. There was a time when they were getting nothing and the $250 was fixed at their request as compensation for the extra cost of the children of the officials of the penitentiary.
The hon. gentleman realizes that the staff in the penitentiary is increasing and the children are increasing.
British Columbia, $56,500.
At L-29 of the Auditor General's Report it will be seen that there was an unusual number of retirements last year. Would the minister explain?

Seven officials retired from the British Columbia penitentiary, Atkins, Bourke, Burr, McKee, McNeill, Mc-Niven and Whyte. McNiven and Burr have since died. McNeill was suspended, but after investigation it was found that the suspension was not justified and he was awarded his retiring gratuity. They are paid one-half month salary for the first five years' service and a full month for each subsequent years in the service.
Is that the only explanation of the extraordinary number?

Atkins retired on account of physical unfitness for service; Bourke retired after the investigation into the escape of certain prisoners; Mr. Burr retired on account of ill-health and died since; Mr. McNeill retired, as I have explained, and Mr. McNiven and Mr. Whyte on account of ill-health.

The minister's explanation is not so full as we might have expected. In addition to those to whom gratuities were paid, some permanent guards retired without gratuity. Is there any special reason for the retirement of T. B. Anderson.
The other guards retired voluntarily, because they thought they could do better outside of the penitentiary.
Do I understand the minister to say seriously that that was the reason for the retirement of Mr. Anderson and Mr. Theroux ?
I cannot assign the particular reasons. They were not asked for their resignations and were not dismissed by the department, but resigned voluntarily-

Well, I live at New Westminster and have considerable acquaintance with the affairs of the penitentiary there, and I have very positive information that Mr. Theroux did not retire voluntarily, and that there were very special circumstances connected with the request for his retirement. I would like the minister to inquire, before we proceed further, whether some of these incidents cannot be recalled now.
The only information we have in the department is that he forwarded his resignation, written by himself, to the minister, and that it was accepted.

Well, all I have to say is that the department is far from being

fully informed. Among these gratuities I notice that Mr. Bourke, who is shown by the report of the Minister of Justice to have been a very long time in the service, receives a retiring allowance of only $279.23. The circumstances must be very special to have him so niggardly dealt with.

That is for the period mentioned there, from July 23, 1886, to October 13, 1892. After fifteen years' service in the penitentiary, he becomes entitled to a superannuation allowance, which he is now getting, in addition.
It is a fact, is it not, that Mr. Bourke has an application now before the department for a more substantial retiring allowance ?
Yes.
May I ask what the claim is ?
He wants us to add ten years to his service.

There is another interesting item on this page :
Canadian Detective Bureau, Vancouver: expenses searching for escaped convicts, $2,485.85
I would like some explanation of that.
This was paid for the services of those who were employed in connection with the Bill Miner escape, and those who escaped with him.
I would like the minister to supplement that by stating whether there were any results from their search ?
We heard about a month ago that they would probably be apprehended before long.
According to an answer given in this House the other day, Bill Miner escaped on the 8th of August. Might I ask when this detective bureau were instructed in this matter.
They were instructed on the 15th day of August. The letter of instructions left on that date.
What was the reason for the delay ?
We wanted to get Bill Miner's portrait printed, so that they would not be working at random. We had a lithograph made, and when It was ready, we sent it with the instructions.

On page L-31 I find this item:
Lieutenant-Colonel A. P. Sherwood, commissioner of police, Ottawa: detective services. $150.
Was that also in connection with the Bill Miner case ?
Yes.
And the commissioner of police was instructed when?
On the 12th day of August, the day we heard in Ottawa that Bill Miner had escaped.
The hon. minister is in error there, because that does not agree with the answer given the other day, that the department heard on the 9th of August that Bill Miner had escaped.
They heard on the 8th that four convicts had escaped, and on the 12th they learned that Bill Miner was one of the four.

In the annual report of the minister we read this at page 2:
The unusual number of escapes is a matter of extreme regret. All occurred at British Columbia penitentiary, and were due to general lack of discipline and to disregard of the prison regulation. The staff of the penitentiary has been reorganized, and several subsequent attempts to mutiny and escape have been frustrated. The tendency of some officers to act upon their individual judgment, in defiance of the established regulations, which are the product of decades of experience, invariably leads to disastrous results. The superior officer who disregards the instructions and regulations by which he is governed cannot enforce obedience from subordinates who naturally exercise the same private judgment in the discharge of their duties. The successful commander is he who has first learned to obey.
This paragraph charges general insubordination and neglect of duty or worse in the British Columbia penitentiary. I submit that when we are called upon to pass the estimates for the support of that institution, we are entitled to have a serious explanation from the minister in charge of it, and I ask him now to make a fuller explanation than has been made respecting the condition of affairs shown by this report to have existed in that institution.

I understand that at the time of the escape of Bill Miner, Bourke, the deputy warden, was acting as warden, and did not keep the discipline he ought to have kept, and it was for that reason that the escape took place. Now Mr. Bourke has disappeared, a new warden has been appointed, and the reorganization is complete.

I do not think that is exactly a satisfactory explanation. The case of Bill Miner was a specially notorious one in British Columbia, and indeed in the whole of western Canada. The man had held up railway trains, his exploits had attracted unusual attention on the other side of the line, and flattering references were made to the expeditious way in which justice was meted out to this man. Yet he

escaped on the 8th of August and the department responsible for the penitentiary did not know until the 12th of August that he had escaped, and did not take steps to recapture him until a week afterwards, when it was practically impossible to catch him.

When the officer in charge of the penitentiary wired of the escape he did not mention any names. He just said four prisoners had escaped. It was only on the twelfth that we had the name of Bill Miner mentioned in any despatch to the department. Immediately we gave instructions to try and recapture him if possible.
When the inspector reports upon these penitentiaries, to whom does the report go? Does it go to the Solicitor General or to the Minister of Justice?
It goes to the Minister of Justice.
It is the Minister of Justice who would be informed of this, if any minister were informed?
Certainly.

I am sorry to take up the time of the committee but I am afraid I must supply some of the details as to which the persons responsible for reporting these matters to the department have been so reticent. It has been common report in British Columbia for a long time that Bill Miner did not escape in the ordinary way, that his departure from the British Columbia penitentiary was connived at by persons high in the service of this country. That remained as a matter of mere report until very lately when this arraignment of the officers of the British Columbia penitentiary anpeared in the report of the Minister of Justice. The retort to this was the statement by Mr. Bourke, the late deputy warden who had been retired, that he had in this connection some sensational and far reaching disclosures to make, and he added in a subsequent interview that Bill Miner did not escape from the British Columbia penitentiary but was virtually handed out, and that the other three prisoners were permitted to escape in order to cover up the Miner transaction. This statement has been made in the public press by Mr. Bourke. the late deputy warden. It was made a subject of inquiry by me in this House on the 1st of February, and the answer to my question was an intimation that the inspector had written to Mr. Bourke asking him to make the sensational disclosures which he indicated. But here is where the weak point of the procedure comes in; when we turn to Mr. Bourke's statement we find that the very man who asks him for the report is the man whom he charges with knowing something more about this affair than has been Mr. BURRELL.	'
communicated to the department. I read in the New Westminster ' Columbian ' of the 28th of January this statement said to have been made by Mr. Bourke:
Editor ' Daily Columbian.'
Sir,-Under the heading ' Dispatch from Ottawa gives wrong information,' appears an item in a local paper of to-day. Wrong impressions, where the escape of Bill Miner is hinted at, seem to he in order. Indeed right impressions of anything connected with the penitentiary service are about as rare as angels' visits; for, if a few good men were to retire, truth might be reckoned there among the lost arts.
It was my hope that when I tendered my resignation justice would be done me. It was also my hope that I would be allowed to spend the balance of my days in comparative quietness. These hopes are vanished. Justice has not been done me in the matter of my retiring allowance, and there is evidently a desire to pursue me into retirement with a spirit worse than vindictive. The secrets that I intended to keep must therefore become public. I have written to Ottawa for a report of the Minister of Justice, and if I find the reports to the press of this province correct, I shall open up a new field for moral reformers in which the evils, as compared with those in the old fields will be found as 16 to 1, that is, if moral reformers have courage enough to investigate.
He then proceeds to refer to some other matters which I need not read.
Mr. Bourke returned to the charge on the 3rd of February.
Who is the editor of that paper you are quoting from?
That is immaterial.
For the information of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gordon) I may tell him that I, when I am at home, am the editor of that paper, and that I am not ashamed of it.
Hear, hear.
And it is Bourke's own statement you are reading?
Certainly, these are Mr. Bourke's statements, and I think the merriment of the hon. gentlemen opposite is very much out of place in the midst of an indictment like this.
Where is the indictment?

Where is the indictment?' asks the Solicitor General. What have we to hope from such a department of government when the second highest officer in the department having heard the charge that Bill Miner did not escape but was handed out from the penitentiary of New Westminster, returns the answer; Where is the indictment?
Bourke was in charge when he was handed out.

Mr. Bourke returns to the charge in this way:
I have just received the blue book and find your quotation as given in the ' Columbian ' a few days ago
Will my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) allow me a question?
Certainly.
Is this the Mr. Bourke who was in charge of the penitentiary at New Westminster at the time of the escape of Bill Miner?
Yes, sir, this is the same Mr. Bourke who was in charge of the penitentiary, and he is therefore in a position to know what went on within the walls of that institution.
And he is a man who was .under oath to keep good guard of the prisoners in the penitentiary.

If the Solicitor General will kindly permit me to proceed without interrupting me I think I shall be able to show before I conclude that there is good ground for him to believe that persons who are nearer to him have also been dis-regardEul of their oaths in this connection. Mr. Bourke proceeds to say in this second statement:
I have just received the blue book and find, your quotation, as given in the ' Columbian ' a few days ago, correct. The die is now cast. The inspectors have" left me no choice. I must remain under the cloud which they and their satellites have generated over me or appeal to the public. It may be said I should ask for an investigation. The value of an investigation depends entirely on the character and honour of the man conducting it From long experience and close observation of penitentiary investigations I am sorry to have to say I have not to-day one shred of confidence in them. A penitentiary investigation appears to me as a man clothed with authority to find out certain facts. He goes to work with a whitewash brush in one hand and a tar brush in the other and seeks diligently for everything but the facts required. If by any chance he finds these facts he applies the brush-the whitewash to those he likes, the tar to those he dislikes.
I have another objection to such investigations. I am strongly of opinion that their frequency and methods connected with them are largely responsible for the demoralized condition of that service.
Then he proceeds to moralize, which it is not necessary for me to read, and he concludes in this way:
The Bill Miner case alone would not give this opportunity. It is but an incident. I shall begin at once to collect and arrange my facts and when this is done which will probably be in a few weeks, I shall hand all to the press.
I submit that this statement by Mr. Bourke, which seems to have been brought 30

to the attention of the department here, calls for a serious report to this House regarding the facts connected with this occurrence in British Columbia and as to what the department knows about it. The current report at New Westminster-for which I do not vouch because there is no way by which we can verify it except by the department giving us the facts in it3 possession-has been published in the press from time to time, as current news of this kind usually is, and that current report is to the effect that Bill Miner in his first train robbery-because he committed two in British Columbia-secured a quantity of valuable securities, and that the owners of these bonds endeavoured to induce him to state what he had done with them, but that he refused to make any communication unless he was released. Further, that certain persons, presumably detectives, were permitted to visit him in the penitentiary on several occasions before he escaped, or appeared to escape; that these persons were still in New Westeminster when he did escape, and that a few weeks before his escape his hair and moustache were allowed to grow, and at a later period he was allowed freedom from the interior of the prison, where criminals of his character are confined, and given the comparative liberty of the brick yard.
Did Mr. Bourke state or insinuate anything of that kind?
I think I am making a statement so serious that I should not be interrupted. Mr. Bourke did not say that, so far as I know, but I say that it is common report.
Mr. Bourke will not say so.

It is common report, and if the hon. gentleman has any further information it is his duty to disclose it. Before I have done with this business I propose to ask for an inquiry, and if that inquiry is granted, I shall see that the hon. gentleman is summoned as a witness. But in the meantime I would ask him not to interrupt the proceedings. The current report is that the very afternoon Miner escaped the fact was wired to the department at Ottawa and when the next day no answer was received, another message was sent to the department urging it to give a prompt reply and asking that a liberal reward be offered for his recapture. Not only one, but three, four, five and six days passed before the department at Ottawa was heard from and before a reward was offered; and when a reward was offered it was the paltry sum of $500 for the recapture of a desperado known all over the North American continent and whose liberty would be cheap to him at ten times that sum.
And his moustache was so grown you would not recognize him.

Apparently the hon. gentlemen who sit behind and support those responsible for the Justice Department see nothing but a subject for a slim joke in the circumstances I have related. I ask these hon. gentlemen who treat this as a joke if there be any crime in the calendar which they would condemn, when they treat as a matter for merriment the allegation that by the use of a golden key you may unlock the door of a penitentiary and allow to escape a criminal who had committed an offence so grave that pardon for it was out of the question. I am surprised that this matter should be treated in a spirit of levity by any one in this House. This escape of Miner is unique in this respect, that he was the only prisoner who ever got away from British Columbia with the exception of two halfbreeds who escaped from Wright's island, and one of them was recaptured a few days ago. Before this episode, such a thing as a clean getaway was unknown, because escaped prisoners were always caught again. We have in these rumours, all of which have found their way into the press, and in the personal statement of ex-Deputy Warden Bourke that Bill Miner did not escape, but was handed out, sufficient grounds for an investigation, not only into the management of the penitentiary, but into the connecting links between the Department of Justice and the penitentiary at Westminster, and we are entitled to be informed how it is that grave incidents connected with the visit of the inspector previous to the departure of Bill Miner were not reported to this department.
Does the hon. gentleman make the statement that shortly prior to the. escape of Bill Miner there was a visit of the inspector to the penitentiary?
I have it in the Auditor General's Report here, which gives the date of the visit
I am not disputing the statement. I did not understand what the hon. gentleman said.

I verified it from the Auditor General's Report before mentioning it in this House. The reason I asked if there was any particular incidents connected with the retirement of a couple of the guards shortly prior to Miner's escape, is because the story is current that one of those guards was found to have addressed to him a communication for Bill Miner, enclosing money, and that in consequence of this discovery he was told to resign; yet we are told now this man resigned voluntarily and his resignation was accepted.
Does the hon. gentleman know the name of the guard?

His name was Ter-roux and I have personal information as to the cause of his retirement. A close friend of his came to me, as a newspaper man in New Westminster, and begged that if we heard anything about his retirement we should not publish it because the poor fellow had been caught in the indiscretion of doing a little for a prisoner and was told he should resign. Later on it was alleged that he was acting as the go-between between some one on the outside of the penitentiary and Bill Miner. My information was that when the Terroux incident was reported, the inspector was actually present in the penitentiary, and that was what led me to ask in this House the other day whether the department had any knowledge of any communication from outside the penitentiary with convict Miner prior to his escape. The answer given me was 'No,' which would indicate that this incident of a receipt of a money letter by Miner was not communicated to the department; that the report was wrong that detectives were permitted to go into the cell and interview Miner there.
The answer I have received gives the contradiction to the story of the detectives which I have mentioned here to-night. I am aware of the discrepancy between this statement and that of the late deputy warden of New Westminster. But I say the situation is so grave, the whole chain of circumstances connected with Bill Miner's escape was so suspicious, even before that ex-deputy warden came forward with his extraordinary statements, that there is serious ground for some kind of inquiry so that this matter may be disposed of. I think the Minister of Justice cannot afford to let an incident like this be dismissed with a laugh on the part of his supporters. I do not think the Minister of Justice could have had the slightest suspicion of any thing of this kind having occurred without taking drastic measures immediately. 1 have confidence in the integrity of the head of that department. But the answer I have-received here, and on a former occasion, leads me to believe that his subordinates have not conveyed to him the information which he should have received. Therefore I ask the minister, as the responsible head of the department to take steps to make a full inquiry and to see that the inquiry is conducted by some other person than the inspector who is now writing to Mr. Bourke, but who stands arraigned on the grave statement of Mr. Bourke to the public press.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall not attempt to make an answer to the observations of the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Taylor), as I have not been able to hear them. But I

welcome the opportunity to make to this committee a statement of the circumstances connected with the escape of this particular convict. I should say first that it was not only the only escape that had taken place that summer from this institution. The warden, Col. White, a gentleman who had been in charge of the penitentiary in British Columbia for many years, was at that time unable to discharge the duties of his position, from a serious illness which not only confined him to his room and his bed, but made it impossible to communicate with him on matters of business, and which afterwards turned out to be his final illness. In consequence of that illness the care and charge of the institution had devolved upon the deputy warden. Mr. Bourke had been an official in the service from 1886; he was a man, at all events of long experience, who had gone from the penitentiary in Manitoba to the penitentiary in British Columbia, and was a trusted official of the public service. There had been more than one previous escape that summer under circumstances which, at all events, seemed to indicate that there was * a looseness of discipline, a lack of care, an absence of proper instructions to the guards in such a responsible position, and having charge of men of the character of convicts. After these previous escapes had taken place I was not a little taken aback, I am willing to admit, when, on the evening of 8th of August, 1907, a telegram was received from Mr. Bourke stating that four prisoners had escaped, giving no names, giving no particulars, and no indication of what was being done, or could be done, if anything could be done, to effect a recapture. The inspector, Mr. Dawson, was at that time upon official duties in Kingston, Ontario. The other inspector, Mr. Stewart, was in Ottawa; and he and I consulted with reference to what should be done with regard to the condition of things which appeared to exist in British Columbia. We did not doubt that without toy instructions from Ottawa there would be at once every possible effort made by the acting warden, and by the guards and officials in charge of the institution, in so far as guards could be spared, to scour the country in every direction, and to make every possible effort to effect a recapture. I do not doubt that that was done. I did not doubt, upon the reports which subsequently were received, that every possible exertion was made by Mr. Bourke and those who were acting under him, to discover traces of the escaped ^prisoners and to effect a recapture. And I attributed to the excitement that such an occurrence necessarily would cause, and to the efforts which were undoubtedly made by all who were in charge to secure the recapture of the prisoners, if possible-I attributed I say, to that circumstance the fact that no 30i
additional communication came from Mr. Bourke on the subject until the 12th of August. But the extent of the message which then came, and which for the first time gave the slightest hint that Miner was one of those that had escaped, was a telegram which Mr. Bourke despatched on the 11th of August. When it reached Ottawa it was not addressed, as it ought to have been, and as I understand Mr. Bourke says his original message was addressed, to the inspectors, but it was addressed to Mr. Dawson individually. On receipt at Ottawa, instead of being delivered to me, or to Mr. Stewart, or to the department, it was repeated to Mr. Dawson at Kingston, and for that reason there was a delay in the delivery of that telegram of some hours, over night, and possibly some portion of a day. But immediately on that telegram being sent by Mr. Dawson to Mr. Stewart, and upon its reaching Ottawa, and upon my becoming acquainted with the fact that Miner was one of those that had escaped, I sent for Mr. Sherwood, the commissioner of Dominion police, and directed him at once to offer a reward for the apprehension of Miner, and to communicate immediately with a man who had recently been in the service, Mr. Chamberlain, of the Dominion Police, who had a few months before gone to Vancouver, and who was there in the position, I think, of chief of police for that city. That was done. Col. Sherwood acted with promptness, and without loss of even one hour. From the time when the first intimation came to us at Ottawa that Miner had escaped, every possible exertion was made, in the offer of a reward, and in securing the services of the best man we knew who could be obtained for the work, Mr. Chamberlain, to endeavour to assist the officials of the penitentiary to discover some traces of the escaped prisoners. These efforts turned out to be unavailing, the prisoners who escaped on that afternoon have not been found up to the present time. A reward was offered, the search continued until it was useless to search longer. Looking back after the event, and with the memory of the depositions which afterwards were taken, and of the exertions which were afterwards made by the officials, I am not able to see in any respect how any thing more could have been done after the escape had taken place by any of the officials of the penitentiary or of the department, in the effort to retrieve the misfortune which had fallen upon the institution and upon the country by the escape.
Mr. Dawson was sent at the earliest moment he could be spared from his duties in Eastern Canada to New Westminster to take charge of the institution. He arrived there on the 27th August. At once, in his

capacity as inspector, he assumed charge of the institution. He remained there until some time in the following December endeavouring to put that institution upon a more satisfactory footing in matter of discipline, in the matter of reorganization, and in endeavoring to find out by a long, patient, painstaking investigation what the trouble was and what was the explanation of the numerous escapes which had taken place during that summer. That investigation was conducted by Mr. Dawson under oath, exercising the powers which the Penitentiary Act confers upon him. The depositions of the witnesses were forwarded to Ottawa, -were carefully examined by myself and are on the files of the department. As a result of that investigation in which a most careful effort was made to ascertain the whole truth of this matter, and to find out if possible, where the blame lay, it was thought that there must be some change in the management of the institution. Four prisoners scarcely walk out of a penitentiary or escape through a hole dug under the palisade in open daylight under the very eyes of guards or officials without there being somebody to blame. Mr. Bourke now speaks of the use of a whitewash brush or of a tar brush in every investigation, and speaks as if it were a question as to which had been applied to the officials in this case. I can only say that certainly no tar brush was applied to Mr. Bourke. He was the man in charge, the responsibility rested primarily and to a greater extent upon him than upon any one else. I do not mean that his eye was watching when the escape took place, but it was his duty, his business, his power and right, to assign the different gangs of convicts to the different guards about the institution. It was he who directed where the men were to work upon any given day, what guard, or guards, were to be in charge, who stationed the officials and who was, in that sense, responsible. Mr. Bourke's resignation was not demanded. Mr. Bourke was not dismissed. Mr. Bourke was allowed to retire and was given his retiring allowance calculated upon the full basis of his service. He thought that the rule which, in some instances, had been, years ago, applied to officials in the service by which, in calculating the amount of their superannuation or retiring allowance, ten years was added to their actual period of service, ought to have been applied to in his case. He asked that ten years should be added to his years of service for the purpose of computing his superannuation or retiring allowance. I had to tell him that that had never been [DOT]done by this government, that, as a matter of policy, I, at any rate, was opposed to the whole pension system and that in so far as his proposition was concerned I [DOT]could not recommend the granting of what Mr. AYLESWORTH.
he asked. Mr. Bourke, in his letters to the newspapers on this subject says, according to one of the clippings before me, that his quarrel in this matter-he calls it his quarrel-is with the inspectors. He says:
My quarrel is with the employees and the officials of penitentiary service, not with the government or Minister of Justice.
Mr. Bourke has a grievance. Mr. Bourke complains that ten years was not added to his service in addition to the actual number of years that he had served in computing his retiring allowance or superannuation. I can only attribute to his feeling of not being dealt with as he thinks he ought to have been the course which he has recently seen fit to take in regard to this matter. He takes offence, or he objects to the remarks which have been made by the inspectors in their annual report, and which have been referred to. That language is, as it purports to be, the language of the inspectors themselves. They say in their report to me:
The unusual number of escapes is a matter of extreme regret. All occurred at British Columbia penitentiary, and were due to general lack of discipline and to disregard of the prison regulations. The staff of the penitentiary has been reorganized, and several subsequent attempts to mutiny and escape have been frustrated. The tendency of some officers to act upon their individual judgment, in defiance of the established regulations, which are the product of decades of experience, invariably leads to disastrous results. The superior officer who disregards the instructions and regulations by which he is governed cannot enforce obedience from subordinates who naturally exercise the same right of private judgment in the discharge of their duties. The successful commander is he who has first learned to obey.
I did not pen these words. I read them, they were put before me, I approved them then and I approve them now. I think the circumstances called for at least that amount of comment. But, Mr. Bourke, seeing these statements or comments in the report of the inspectors, appears to have rushed into the newspapers; in fact, if I am to credit the statements which he makes in either an interview or a signed letter published in the Daily ' Columbian ' of New Westminster on the 3rd of February, he is appealing to public opinion to right him in this matter. I can only say that, seeing as I did on the 29th of January, in the Eastern Canadian newspapers, a telegraphic item that Mr. Bourke stated that he was in a position to make sensational disclosures, I immediately, upon my reaching Ottawa, having read this statement on the train coming to Ottawa, instructed the inspectors to communicate with Mr. Bourke and to demand-to demand as a right- that he should put the department in pos-

session of any information whatever which he had. It is true that Mr. Bourke gave evidence in this matter while the occurrences were fresh. Mr. Bourke was examined at great length before Mr. Dawson in the investigation which took place in the fall of 1907 and while the events were fresh in the minds of everybody. His evidence is upon file in the department and he was sworn not only to answer the questions that were put to him, but to tell the whole truth in regard to this matter. If, notwithstanding his duty as an official of the department and the oath under which he was testifying, he kept back material circumstances which he did not then disclose, it seems to me the disclosure of those circumstances now will come from him with far less weight than if he had told them when under oath to tell the whole truth. Mr. Bourke was written to on January 30 in these terms :
Dear Sir,-An item appeared in a few of the Ontario newspapers yesterday stating that you are in a position to make disclosures regarding the escape of Bill Miner on August 8, 1907.	_	.
For the information of the minister will you please furnish us at once with a statement of any information you may possess regarding the matter, that you have not already disclosed ?
That letter has not yet, I suppose, had time, in the course of post, to produce an answer here; at all events no answer has yet come. But Mr. Bourke in the meantime has not thought fit to keep silent; he has communicated to the newspapers in the way indicated and yesterday copies of the British Columbia newspapers of February 3, containing the substance of interviews with him or articles written by him reached Ottawa and were seen by me. I refer only to one thing in the communication which the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the committee has in part, or possibly in whole, read. Mr. Bourke speaking of investigations, says:
I have another objection to such investigations. I am strongly of opinion that their frequency and the methods connected with them are largely responsible for the demoralized condition of that service.
I do not know to what Mr. Bourke refers in speaking of frequency. I had not been in charge of the Department of Justice much more than a year when this investigation took place in the fall of 1907, but I have asked those who have been connected with the department for many years in regard to the frequency of investigations referred to by Mr. Bourke and I am told that for more than twelve years there had never been a single investigation in the penitentiary of British Columbia, or occasion for it. until these repeated and numerous escapes in the summer of 1907 called for investigation and inquiry. In these circumstances I am at a loss to understand what is meant by this allusion to these frequent investigations, and I can only say in regard to the attitude which Mr. Bourke has seen fit to take in this whole matter, that if he had communicated directly with the department, either upon the occasion of the escape itself, or upon the occasion of the subsequent investigation, or upon the occasion of his application for a retiring allowance and superannuation or at this date, and before he had resorted to the newspapers for his vindication his representations would have received the most careful attention and consideration which it was in my power to give.
Allusions are made, hints are thrown out,
I do not know but statements have been made, it may be that it has been in so many words charged that this was no real escape on the part of the malefactor Miner, that this was something connived at, something assisted by some one in connection with the institution, or some one of the authorities. I can say nothing in that respect except what I know. When a general charge is levelled at everybody at large and it is said that somebody connived, somebody assisted, somebody helped,
I do not know who is meant. I can speak for myself at all events and I think I can speak for the officials of the penitentiaries branch of the Department of Justice and repudiate any such insinuation and say that there is not one word, one breath, of foundation for it. Reference is made I understand, to some rumour or story or canard to the effect that there were bonds hidden, stolen property, the secret of whose hiding place was known to Miner and that there was some arrangement, understanding, proposition or suggestion that if there were disclosure of that secret by him his escape would be winked at, he would be allowed to go. There was some allusion to such a thing by some witnesses in the investigation to which I referred. An effort was made to trace the thing up to find if there was the remotest ground or reason under the sun for thinking that any such thing had taken place. It was investigated, so far as was possible to investigate such a shadowy vague and unsubstantial rumour, and it was found to be exactly what I described, absolutely unfounded. If Mr. Bourke has information in regard to the existence of any such understanding, I wish certainly that he would make it known. It is my desire, it must be the desire of every member of this committee, it must be the desire of every citizen of this country who has its welfare or the enforcement of its laws at heart that if there be the slightest reason for supposing even that such a thing is a fact, those reasons should be known and the matter should be put

before this House and before the public. I hope at any rate that if Mr. Bourke is possessed of any information whatever which he has not already disclosed he will respond to the demand which has been made upon him and give us the benefit of that information at once.
There has not been on the part of the department here or of the inspectors or of myself or any one in authority at Ottawa, any delay any laxity, any resting on our oars ; from the very hour when the first knowledge that action was taken and everything was done that could be done in the effort to find the man and to restore him to the institution from which he had gene.

I would like to contrast the very interesting and important statement just made by the minister with the manner in which we were endeavoured to be put off by the Solicitor General when I raised this question an hour ago. I would like to put it to the committee if the statement just made by the Minister of Justice does not warrant the course I took in insisting that we should have an explanation upon this subject. If it does not condemn the attitude of the Solicitor General, who must have known the facts which have just been stated to the House by the Minister of Justice and yet deliberately concealed them from this committee when challenged and invited over and over again by me to give an explanation on this subject

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must not use the term ' deliberately conceal ' in the House.

If I have gone beyond the bounds of parliamentary decorum, Mr. Chairman, I withdraw the term ' deliberately concealed ' from the House, but I wish to say that when an hon. minister is entrusted with the duty of putting estimates through this House, and gives answers as of his own knowledge to questions put to him by a member of the House, he should at least be posted; and that we are entitled to view with distrust other statements when we find him deliberately disposing of a great question like this with the statement that there is nothing in it, in view of the fact that the answer of the Minister of Justice a few moments afterwards shows that there is a great deal in it, and that the department was fully informed on it when the Solicitor General was not. I would like, to correct the hon. Minister of Justice on one point. He says that this was not the first escape from the British Columbia penitentiary, but was only one of a series of escapes. That is an error. The report of his own department shows that there were only six escapes during the year-these four and two subsequently from Wright's Island near the New Westminster peniten-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: tiary. There were no previous escapes from that penitentiary, so far as I know, or as indicated by the report. To that extent the minister appears to have been misinformed. I would like to call attention to the fact that the most grave passages of the story which I have related to this House have not been dealt with. For instance, the current report in New Westminster is that the guard Theroux was dismissed or ordered to resign because he was found passing communications from the outside to Miner. That has not been dealt with at all, and I submit that we are entitled to an answer as to that. There is also the further report that certain detectives were interviewing Bill Miner. That is either so or not so; I do not know; it is currently reported in New Westminster and that too has not been answered. If we had the positive assurance of the minister that the department never gave permission to any person to go in there and interview Miner, it would do a great deal to clear up the cloud that hangs over this transaction. We have also heard nothing from the hon. minister as to the suggestion that there should be an impartial inquiry into this affair, because, as we have seen, the only answers that have been made so far have been made by the inspector, the very person whom the ex-deputy warden accuses; and therefore, even if he is as innocent as an unborn babe, even if this charge of the ex-deputy warden is simply from pique that his demand for a greater gratuity is not acceded to, it is not proper that the inquiry should be at the hands of the person accused. We should have some statement as to what course the department intends to take, and therefore I woultl suggest that this item should stand until the minister can read ' Hansard ' and learn what has been said here, post himself on the facts and make a statement to this committee.

I would not be disposed to attach too much credit to statements such as have emanated from Mr. Bourke, seeing that he has had an oppor-, tunity already of giving evidence upon oath and making known any of the alleged facts to which he alludes in his recent statements to the newspapers. The Minister of Justice in speaking of the communication to Mr. Bourke, said that he had demanded from him, not as of grace, but as of right, full information respecting the facts to which Mr. Bourke had made allusion. When we heard the letter read, it did not seem to me that it quite bore out the view of the minister in that regard, because it was couched in the terms of a very polite request rather than of a distinctly stern demand upon this man to make known matters which must have come to his knowledge as an official of the government of this country, if at all. It was: ' Will you please give information

to the department of any of these matters to which you are alluding ? ' It does not seem to me that this is the way in which the government of this country should deal with a man who had made statements of that kind. He was the deputy warden, the acting warden, in charge of this penitentiary at the time the escape took place. Mr. Bourke has said either too much or too little, and I think the answer that ought to be given to him by the government as those responsible to this parliament, would be to summon him at once before a committee of this House to tell upon oath all he knows of this matter. That is the only way to deal with a man who has made the very grave statements that apparently he has made in the newspaper press. This is due to the government, the parliament and the people of this country; because so long as statements of this kind go abroad and remain uninvestiagted or are treated with indifference, they are bound to bring the administration of justice-and the punishment of offenders is strictly a part of it-into contempt. I therefore suggest to the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General that they should take at once into their grave and serious considerations whether this man should not be brought before a committee of this House, and the statements which he has made so frequently in the public press tested by a thorough strict and stern examination of him upon oath in order that he either withdraw or make good.

Replying to the hon. leader of the opposition, I may state that his suggestion will have careful consideration. He knows my position and the position of the Minister of Justice. I do not form part of the Cabinet, and if he will allow me to confer with the minister, I have no doubt the request will be granted. As to my hon. friend, who is the editor of a paper in New Westminster, I am surprised at the attitude he takes when he says I deliberately concealed information which I had from the House. He has no ground for that statement. He asked for the reasons why So-and-So was retired. I gave the information as I had it from the officer in charge of the institution. I have no apology to make for my conduct to this House. I have never tried to conceal or hide anything. Whatever answers I gave were true answers, giving the information that was conveyed to me. As to the details of Miner's escape, the hon. member never asked me to go into the history of it or tell him what passed between the government and the officials. To the questions put I gave the answers. He asked if we had heard any news about Miner. I told him exactly the information as conveyed to me by tne inspector. He asked what the mone.v wras used for. I stated for the purpose?
indicated in the Auditor General's Report. The hon. gentleman comes with bad grace to claim that we are trying to conceal anything or that we are not true to our trust before the House when he takes common report from the streets, when he takes the stuff he fills his paper with.
The hon. gentleman takes common rumour and sets that against the statement of a man examined under oath. He does this to suit his purpose, and it comes with bad grace from one who will do this, to throw suspicion on the honesty and the loyalty of those who represent the Department of Justice. My answer to questions on the estimates, I admit, may not be as clear as they should be, and I admit that I may at times weary some members of the committee by asking them to repeat their questions, but my hon. friend must not forget that when I am talking English I am not talking my mother tongue, and I think that there is sufficient patience and courtesy in this House to bear with me under the circumstances. At times I may make use of a word which is not technically correct, but when I do so, I do not think that warrants any hon. gentleman in taking advantage of my lack of knowledge and saying that 1 have given an offensive answer or have tried to deceive the House. And when my attention is drawn to any slip I may inadvertently make, I think I can rely on the kindness of my neighbour to tell me what is the proper word to use. The hon. member for New Westminster tried to throw a cloud over an official of the Department of Justice, the inspector, Mr. Dawson. The hon. gentleman insinuates that there must have been some connivance between some officer high in authority in the administration of our penitentiaries and the convict Miner. But how could there be any connivance be tween the authorities in Ottawa and the officials in New Westminster? How could there be any plot and conspiracy except by writing or wire? I submit further to the fairness of this committee, who would have been the man at the other end of the line, on the Pacific coast, to hold the strings and be the chief medium in any connivance with the officials in Ottawa? It would certainly be the man highest in authority in the administration of the penitentiaries, Mr. Bourke. And if Mr. Bourke knew that the officials in Ottawa were not doing their duty, if he knew that they were trying to have Miner escape, and did not disclose that when under oath, why does not Mr. Bourke-who wants now to take the public into his confidence and show them how badly he was treated by the department- and what a rascal is the inspector of penitentiaries-why does he not now produce those lettefs published in my hon. friend's paper? I suppose the reason is that he has not got them. There can be no other reason. I am sure he has not got them. I know, from the knowledge I have of the

administration of the Department of Justice, that not a shadow of suspicion ought to be cast on Mr. Dawson the inspector of penitentiaries. There is no man in the whole service who stands higher in the esteem of his chief and of all concerned with the administration of the department than does Mr. Dawson, and I repeat there is no ground for the suspicion cast upon him by the hon. member for New Westminster to-night. If the hon. gentleman has any charges to make, let him make them. It is his duty to do so. If he has any proof, it is his duty to make a charge, and show that among our officials, in whom we have every confidence, there are men who are betraying their trust, and in this way he will give us an opportunity to inquire into the facts and see that justice is meted out.
The hon. gentleman said that just shortly prior to Miner's escape, one of our inspectors had visited the penitentiary. Well, it was the time for his yearly visit. It was in the month of June, when he went to New Westminster to inspect the penitentiary, as he does in that month every year. During that time, the hon. gentleman insinuates, Theroux had letters and money for Miner.
In this way the hon. gentleman tried to convey the impression that the inspector was in connivance with all those people to procure Miner's escape. And all his insinuations are based on what he calls public rumours. In this way he tries to connect the inspector of penitentiaries with what he says was not an escape but the handing out of a prisoner.
The hon. gentleman insists upon the fact that there were detectives who visited the convict Miner shortly prior to his escape. Well. I am informed that there were, but what was the reason? Miner was arrested for the Kamloops hold-up. The detectives wanted him to give evidence on the Mission hold-up because they thought he knew something about it, and in fact was the guilty party. In this attempt to seek information and discover the culprit, I see nothing reprehensible. That is done in every penitentiary when we believe that convicts can give important information which will lead to the discovery and arrest of criminals.
When did the visits of these detectives take place?

During the twelve months that proceeded Miner's escape, I am told by the inspector that there were several visits made to him, but that convicts are not allowed to see any one alone. Consequently in every one of these visits the detectives were accompanied by the warden or deputy warden. In this case Mr. Dwight was present with the detectives who visited Miner.
What was the date of the last visit?

I cannot say definitely. The information is given from memory only. But the last interview between Miner and the detectives was in the presence of the warden Dwight; and as he was ill quite a few months prior to Miner's escape, I could not give the exact date.

Would my hon. friend be good enough to give any information with regard to another fact which was mentioned, and which seems to have some significance, if well founded. I refer to the dismissal of a guard for the alleged offence of having been the means of communication between persons outside and the convict Miner inside the penitentiary?

As far as the department is concerned, the only information we have is the letter of Theroux and there is nothing in that letter stating that his resignation was asked. He sent in his resignation. There is nothing on the files, nor any letters showing that his resignation has been asked for. He had sent in his resignation.
Was that during Mr. Bourke's regime.
I cannot tell from memory; it was sent in in June or July and it was accepted at once.
It is important to know whether it was when Mr. Bourke was in charge.

I am not as familiar with this matter as is the Minister of Justice, and I will confer with him and get all the information I can and convey it to the House. I do not want to have it believed, as my very kind friend (Mr. J. D. Taylor) has insinuated, that if the thing was sifted to the bottom the Solicitor General would be found to have connived at the escape of Bill Miner. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) need not stay awake about that. If the Solicitor General has not conveyed any further information to the House it is due to the fact that the Solicitor General has no further information to convey. There never was on my part any idea of deceiving the House or withholding information from it. I want to say further, that so far as the Department of Justice is concerned, and so far as the Minister of Justice is concerned-and upon that subject I know his views, because we have conferred very often on the question of the officials-there is no man who stands higher and whose character is more above suspicion than Mr. Dawson the inspector who my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Taylor) has been trying by insinuation and innuendo to connect with this escape.
It would be important that the Solicitor General should confer with the Minister of Justice about that particular incident.
What incident?
The incident with reference to the guard Theroux.
I will try and find out the exact state and get all the information available as to why he was permitted to resign.

And whether or not at the time of his resignation it was known to the department here, or to Mr. Bourke, or whoever was in charge of the institution, that he had been guilty of some offence of this character.
I will get all the records of the department and bring them down.
If necessary it would justify communication by telegram with the authorities of the penitentiary in British Columbia.
I will do it.

I would like to correct the Solicitor General in his impression that I attributed to him any knowledge of these circumstances. In fact, I was careful to ask him very early in my remarks whether these reports if made would be made to him or to the Minister of Justice, and he replied that they would be made not to him, but to the Minister of Justice, and, therefore, as I thought, he escaped from the situation altogether. I wish to say also that the Solicitor General is very unjust to me when he insinuated that in any sense I reflected on the manner in which he addressed this House or upon the language he used.
You said I deliberately concealed what I knew.

I am sure that in no remarks I have made to this House have I been guilty of rudeness to any hon. member and much less have I been guilty of so gross an offence as to venture to criticise the English of the Solicitor General whose mother tongue is French and who speaks our language so beautifully. I would like to point out that there is still another point not cleared up in this transaction-and if the Solicitor General would try once or twice more to forget his resentment towards me in that I have drawn from him the very interesting information that we have at last succeeded in extracting-if he would forget that and deal with some of the points I put before him it would be very much more to the purpose. There is this other matter on which I would like to have information, and that is whether or not Miner was prepared for departure from the institution prior to his escape. It is the practice in these institutions that when a convict is about to end his term his hair and moustache are
allowed to grow. The story current there is -and I have never heard it denied and it has not been denied by the Solicitor General to-night-that Miner was prepared in these two particulars to remove all traces of a convict from him. We knew nothing of the bonds before, until the Minister of Justice told us that came out in the investigation. The Solicitor General could not tell us that. The report of the visit of the detectives was only a street rumour before, and now the Solicitor General tells us that also is correct. Then we come to this other feature of the story, and I ask whether or not Miner was prepared for departure from the penitentiary two or three weeks before he actually got out. I renew my suggestion that full information respecting all these things should be given before we pass this item.
The information at our disposal is a sworn statement from the oflicer in charge that Miner's hair was less than three-quarters of an inch long when he left the penitentiary.

As a preliminary to this discussion I put this question to the government a short time ago:
Q. Had the department any knowledge of communication from outside the penitentiary with convict Miner prior to his escape.
A. No.
The statement to the House to-night i3 that detectives visited him on a dozen occasions in the year preceding his escape.
I explained that.
How did you explain it?
These detectives when they go on official duty are not considered strangers; they are on special service.

That reminds me that the minister stated to this committee that these detectives had gone to Miner to ask him whether or not he had committed the Mission hold-up. There was no doubt at all in the mind of any person in British Columbia about that; there was the fact stated that Miner was recognized and was well known as the man who did commit the Mission hold-up. Even if it were not known, I submit to any lawyer in this House whether it is a rational statement to be made that detectives would be permitted to go into a cell to interview a convict to obtain evidence from him to incriminate himself That evidence could not be used against him afterwards.

The name of the detective is Bullock and he was trying to get information about the Mission hold up. My hon. friend says it was common knowledge in British Columbia that Miner was the

guilty one in that. Why did not my hon. friend produce that evidence before the the tribunal which tried him.
He was not tried on that charge.
He was not tried because they did not have the evidence. Why did you not give to those interested in the administration of justice the evidence as to that?
He was not tried on that charge.

They could not try him unless they had the evidence.
Mr. .1. D. TAYLOR. He was tried for an offence committed a year later and convicted for that offence and sentenced to life imprisonment. What more could you do to him?
But he may not have been alone in the Mission hold up.
The story is that these bonds were stolen in the Mission hold up and the Solicitor General bears that out.

Certainly, they were trying to know what had been done about it; they were trying to get evidence. If we folded our arms and did nothing the hon. gentleman would say: look at the Department of Justice, it is doing nothing, our lives are not safe on the street, and the ' Columbian ' would have come out with a warning to the people to carry revolvers and daggers to protect themselves because justice was not administered. But when we try to get information, then we are doing wrong, we are guilty of a connivance with wrong. That may be the hon. gentleman's view, but' I do not agree with him.

The minister stated just now, as I understood him, that these bonds were supposed to have been stolen at the Mission hold up, and he said that certainly we were trying to get information about them. Am I correct?

I am informed that the object of the interview with Bullock was to get information from Miner about the property that was stolen, he went to the same source of information as my hon. friend. He is informed by common rumour that there were Australian bonds among that property, and they were trying to get from Miner whether he had any knowledge of what disposition was being made of the property.
The Solicitor General says, as I understood him, that these detectives were admitted because they were officials.
No, I did not mean that, I said they were on official duty, going there to seek information.
Did they go there at the instance of the government of Canada?

Speaking from memory, these people were trying to investigate this matter at the instance of the railway company, who were then held responsible for the loss by the express company. They were acting on behalf of the company to get all the information they could about the property.

There seems to be more in the suggestion than one would have gathered from the remarks of the Minister of Justice. * We understood from his remarks that this had been investigated and that there was absolutely nothing in it.
Among the officials of the penitentiary.

I gather from the Minister of Justice and from the Solicitor General that the whole blame for the escape of the four prisoners is cast upon the deputy warden. In view of that, and in view of the strictures laid upon that gentleman by the commission, in which they say there was an unusual number of escapes due to that gentleman's lack of discipline and lack of enforcing the prison regulations, acting in defiance of the instructions of the department-in view of all that, I would like to ask the department if they still intend to superannuate that gentleman, and give him the same treatment as would be given to any man who was retired without any stain upon his record. I understand that superannuation can only be given to a man who has discharged his duties satisfactorily and maintains his reputation for integrity and honesty.
There was no charge against his reputation. He was accused of being slack in the observance of penitentiary discipline, but that was nothing against his character.

As representing a constituency in which this robbery took place, I would like to say one word. I want to express the very strong feeling there was throughout the whole of the province at the desperate character of this man's crime, and to ask hon. gentlemen opposite not to treat this whole matter as if it were one in which we were trying to take a party advantage. Hon. gentlemen opposite have no right to assume that I am trying to make party capital out of an incident in regard to which I value the standard of public justice in Canada more highly than I do party advantage. The feeling in that community was of so grave a character that it was participated in by all men regardless of their party affiliations, and I say that we ought to consider this matter as in-

volving the good name of the whole Dominion, and to appreciate that there is a general desire to clear it up in the interest of justice. That in broad daylight so notorious and so desperate a character as Miner was allowed to escape, and apparently, as has been pointed out by my hon. friend, there is evidence to show that that man's hair was allowed to grow in an unusual way, that he was allowed to escape in broad daylight from a penitentiary equipped, as this was, when the moral effect of his capture and his sentence had been so salutary throughout the whole of British Columbia, then I say the matter is sufficiently grave to require that it be probed to the bottom by the department. I do not know this man Bourke, but I agree with the leader of the opposition in saying that either Bourke has said too much or he has said too little.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to insinuate that any of the officials of the department were privy to the escape of Miner ?

If the hon. gentleman can construe any word that has come out of my mouth to-night in such a way as he suggests, he does not understand the King's English. I am speaking on behalf of my constituents, and expressing the moral effect of this whole affair in British Columbia. I say again that this man Bourke has either said too much or too little, and that the matter is so grave that it should be probed. I think the hon. gentlemen opposite should realize that there are many of us in British Columbia who value the standard and reputation of Canadian justice more than we do party advantage.

Referring to the statement of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) to the effect that Mr. Bourke said too much or too little, did that hon. gentleman come to his conclusion from the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor). I wish to put a question to the hon. member for New Westminster. Wil} he undertake to say that Mr. Bourke suggests in any way whatever that the escape of Miner was due to any negligence, improper conduct or connivance of any of the officials of the penitentiary in British Columbia ? I am not here to defend Mr. Bourke. I know Mr. Bourke, or I know of him as a Tory of the Tories. I realize that hon. gentlemen opposite have placed Mr. Bourke in a false light, and I rise for the purpose of protesting against the aspersion which has been cast upon his character. An aspersion has been cast upon his character by reason of the assertions which were made by hon. gentlemen opposite which assertions have been referred to as if they were expressions of opinion by Mr. Bourke himself. The hon. member for New
Westminster went on to explain how it was that Miner had escaped. He read extracts from interviews and letters published in newspapers, from Mr. Bourke and the impression that would be conveyed to the mind of any ordinary hearer is that Mr. Bourke has made these charges. I venture, for one, to say, that Mr. Bourke never made any such charges, that the charges that the hon. member for New Westminster has referred to are charges which were found in the newspaper of which he has been the editor or with which he is connected.

I ask, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Chisholm) is in order in stating that the letters which I read to the House as letters of Mr. Bourke were not letters of Mr. Bourke but fabrications of that newspaper.

I never said anything of the kind. The point of order is entirely too premature. The impression which was conveyed to the House by the remarks of the hon. gentleman was that the sentiments which he expressed were the sentiments of Mr. Bourke.
I ask your ruling, Mr. Chairman, on the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not hear the hon. gentleman's point of order. Would he kindly state it again?

The hon. gentleman stated that whereas I had read to this committee, as statements of Mr. Bourke, the extracts which I did read here, they were not the statements of Mr. Bourke but they were statements of the newspaper with which my name is connected. I say that is a reflection upon my honour as a member of this House.
The hon. gentleman
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wm. Chisholm) has the right to explain before the decision is given on the point of order.

The hon. member for New Westminster objects that I should ascribe certain sentiments to him. I did not ascribe them to him at all, but what I did state was that the remarks that he made in explanation of the escape of Miner, would, under the circumstances convey the impression that Mr. Bourke had given expression to these sentiments. Now, what I said is that he misled the committee -not intentionally
You cannot tell that.

I am willing to grant that it was not done intentionally. But, he misled the committee by quoting

from interviews and letters written by Mr. Bourke, not finding fault in a general way, but interviews and letters which did not contain one single iota of a charge against the penitentiary in any way, shape or form, and then the hon. member for New Westminster supplemented that by a statement of his own.
I ask if this is speaking to the point of order or if it is pressing an argument on another question. We should have the ruling.

If I have trespassed against the rules of the House I certainly withdraw anything I have said of that character. But the point that I am endeavouring to make is that I know Mr. Bourke, and that whatever may be his faults in so far as discipline is concerned, whatever may be his weakness, I know him to be a strong Conservative, a man of honour and integrity, and it is on that ground that I rise up to protest against the impression that is sought to be created in the minds of hon. members of the House by reason of the remarks made by hon. gentlemen opposite. I am quite sure that Mr. Bourke will exclaim 'save me from my friends' when he reads 'Hansard' to-morrow. The hon. member for New Westminster said that a friend of Mr. Bourke came to the newspaper office and suggested that this thing should not be ventilated in the press.
That is not what I said.

Mr. Theroux had said that he did not want to have this thing ventilated in the press, but right at once Mr. Bourke goes to the press himself and supplies the series of articles that appeared in the paper. Let any man read those articles and tell me if he can find in them a single charge against the penitentiary. All that these articles do is to ventilate the grievance of Mr. Bourke because he did not receive superannuation. It is true that Mr. Bourke believes that he is entitled to superannuation. It is true that he says that under a previous administration there is a precedent for granting him the superannuation^ That is a debatable point. It may be that morally he is entitled to it. But, as the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) pointed out, there is no case within his knowledge in which such a procedure had been adopted. The whole point is whether they could add time to the time he had already served in order to entitle him to superannuation. Mr. Bourke does not say that he has been treated unjustly or unfairly, but he does say that he is entitled to superannuation, while the Department of Justice say he is not. Whom are we to follow in this matter? Whom are we to suppose right in the matter? We must Mr. WILLIAM CHISHOLM.
come to the conclusion that the Minister of Justice and the government are right. I merely rose for the purpose of protesting against any aspersion being cast on the character of Mr. Bourke. Whatever may be his weakness as a disciplinarian and as an officer he is a thoroughly honourable man.

I was going to ask hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, as there will be considerable discussion upon this point, to let the item stand as it has been agreed and go on with the items for Alberta. There is only one other item left outside of British Columbia. We can leave that and it will bring us back to the discussion of this matter.
Some resolutions reported.
Hon. Mr. PATERSON moved the adjournment of the House.
Would the leader of the House kindly tell us what will be taken up to-morrow?

If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) returns to-night from the Forestry Convention in Toronto, the resolution standing in his name, dealing with the Civil Service, will be taken up first. If that is disposed of, it will be followed by the estimates of the Indian and Interior Departments. If the Minister of Agriculture is not here then we will go into supply at once on the Indian and Interior estimates of the Railway Department.
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 11.40 p.m.
Friday, February 12, 1909.
